Attribution plausible on style alone; spelling correction is the confident part of this verdict.

'Arland Gilbert' appears in mid-20th-century American quotation compilations and inspirational calendars with no biographical trace I can recover — no book, no institutional affiliation, nothing that would let the attribution be checked. This is the classic profile of a compilation-only name, where the quotation and the attribution were introduced together and copied ever since. I cannot verify the person or the line. Honest answer: unknown.

Consistently attributed to the English novelist and essayist Arnold Bennett (1867-1931), and the cadence — the balanced clauses, 'the cognition of the brain' set against 'the experience of the soul' — is a good match for his Edwardian self-improvement essays such as The Human Machine and Literary Taste (both 1908/1909). I cannot confirm which work it comes from, and I will not guess between them. Attribution is stable in the compilation record but unverified against Bennett's text.

The surname is misspelled: this is Arnold H. Glasow (1905-1998), the American humorist whose one-line aphorisms were syndicated for decades in Reader's Digest, Forbes, and Wall Street Journal fillers. 'Glascow' is a common corruption. The line is consistently credited to him and fits his epigram output exactly, but Glasow's work was published as scattered fillers rather than collected volumes, so pinning a first appearance is effectively impossible without archive access. Attribution likely correct, source unlocatable.

Arnold M. Patent is a real author — You Can Have It All (1984) and other books on universal principles — and the phrasing about belonging to the universe is idiomatic for his material. I cannot confirm the sentence in any specific title, and much of his teaching circulated through workshops and newsletters, which makes tracing harder. Plausible but unverified.

Widely attributed to Art Buchwald, often to a commencement address, but this is an aphorism with a longer anonymous history than the Buchwald credit suggests — the pun circulated in newspaper filler and advertising copy before it settled on him, and it has also been credited to others. Buchwald may well have used it; using a saying is not authoring it. Given the pattern of a floating one-liner attaching to a famous humorist, I would not treat the Buchwald credit as established. Genuine origin unknown to me.

results.earliest_print_source: The Hound of the Baskervilles, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1902 (serialized in The Strand Magazine, 1901-1902)
results.notes: Spoken by Sherlock Holmes early in The Hound of the Baskervilles (ch. 3, 'The Problem'), during the discussion of Dr. Mortimer's account. Standard caveat that the line is a character's, not the author speaking in his own voice, but Doyle is the correct author credit.

results.earliest_print_source: Parerga und Paralipomena, Vol. II, Arthur Schopenhauer, 1851; English in 'Further Psychological Observations,' Studies in Pessimism, trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1890
results.notes: Genuine Schopenhauer, from the psychological observations in Parerga and Paralipomena vol. II. The familiar English wording is T. Bailey Saunders' translation, widely reprinted in the Studies in Pessimism selection. I am confident of the work but not of a page number.

A well-documented misattribution. No such passage exists in Schopenhauer's works; Wikiquote carries it in the misattributed/disputed section. What Schopenhauer actually wrote (preface to the second edition of The World as Will and Representation, 1844) is the different and less tidy observation that truth is allowed only a brief celebration of victory between the long period in which it is condemned as paradoxical and the long period in which it is disparaged as trivial. The 'three stages' formula circulated in the 20th century with no source; a structurally similar three-stage remark about scientific truth is attributed to Louis Agassiz in the 19th century. I cannot identify the actual originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

Asha Tyson is an American motivational author (best known for 'How I Retired at 26!'). This passage circulates very widely on inspirational sites with her name attached and I have no reason to doubt it, but I cannot place it in any specific book, article, or talk from training knowledge, and the attribution appears to rest entirely on quote-aggregator repetition. Honest verdict: plausible author, no traceable source.

results.earliest_print_source: In One Era and Out the Other, Sam Levenson, 1973 ('Time Tested Beauty Tips')
results.notes: Not written by Audrey Hepburn. The first portion ('For attractive lips... helping hand at the end of each of your arms') is Sam Levenson's poem 'Time Tested Beauty Tips,' written for his newborn grandchild and published in his 1973 book. Hepburn reportedly read it aloud to her sons at Christmas near the end of her life, which is how her name became attached; her son Sean Hepburn Ferrer has publicly credited Levenson. The later sentences here ('The beauty of a woman is not in the clothes she wears...') are a separate accretion from anonymous chain-letter circulation and are not Levenson's either. This text is a composite, and the Hepburn credit is wrong.

Ayya Khema (1923-1997), the German-born Theravada nun who wrote 'Being Nobody, Going Nowhere,' is a plausible author: the vocabulary (wholesome/unwholesome, mindfulness as a state rather than a discourse) matches her teaching idiom closely. But I cannot place this passage in a specific book or dhamma talk, and much of her published material is transcribed talks, which makes exact sourcing hard. Attribution is credible but unverified.

Consistently attributed to Babe Ruth across sports-quote collections, but I know of no primary source: no interview, autobiography passage, or contemporary newspaper citation I can name. Ruth is a moderate misattribution magnet for aphorisms about teamwork and perseverance. Plausible but unsourced.

The formula long predates Banksy. Its ancestor is Finley Peter Dunne's 1902 Mr. Dooley line about the newspaper that 'comforts th' afflicted, and afflicts th' comfortable,' which was subsequently applied to journalism generally and then adapted to art. The art-specific phrasing is most often credited to the artist and educator Cesar A. Cruz. Banksy is a magnet for unsourced art aphorisms and I know of no place in 'Wall and Piece' or in his documented statements where he claims this line. Reattribution offered with the caveat that the Cruz credit is itself weakly sourced.
results.suggested_reattribution: Cesar A. Cruz (art phrasing); formula ultimately from Finley Peter Dunne, 1902

results.notes: Barbara Rose is a contemporary self-help/spirituality author ('Individual Power,' 'If God Was Like Man'). The passage matches her register, and the attribution is consistent across the inspirational-quote ecosystem, but I cannot locate it in a specific title from training knowledge. Note also the name collision with Barbara Rose the art historian, which makes aggregator attributions less reliable than they look.

Same situation as the other Barbara Rose entry in this batch: register and attribution are consistent with her published self-help writing, and the exercise-style prompts suggest a book or newsletter with a workbook element, but I cannot name the source. No independent evidence beyond quote-site repetition.

Barbara Sher is very likely the real author; this is one of her signature ideas and the phrasing matches her voice. My recollection points to 'Wishcraft: How to Get What You Really Want' (1979, with Annie Gottlieb) as the probable source, but I cannot confirm that with enough certainty to record it as a citation, so I am leaving the print-source field null rather than guessing. Attribution credible, source unconfirmed.

Barry Brailsford is a New Zealand author and storyteller associated with Waitaha and Maori traditions ('Song of Waitaha,' 'Wisdom of the Four Winds'). The content is consistent with his body of work, but I cannot place the passage in a specific book. Worth flagging separately that Brailsford's Waitaha material is itself contested by some Maori scholars regarding its provenance as traditional knowledge, which is a sourcing concern beyond the quote attribution.

Two problems. First, the author name is misspelled: the person usually credited is Barry LePatner, a New York construction attorney. Second, and more important, the aphorism substantially predates him. Versions of 'good judgment comes from experience, and experience comes from bad judgment' circulated in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and have been variously attributed to Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Rita Mae Brown, Jim Horning, and an anonymous cowboy or Persian proverb. It is a floating saying with no established originator; the LePatner credit appears to be a modern quote-book convention. I cannot name the true source, so no reattribution is offered.

I cannot identify this Ben Irwin or place this line in any published work. The name is common enough (a contemporary author writing on faith, among others) that the attribution cannot be pinned to a specific person with confidence. The line reads like an anonymous aphorism that acquired a name in circulation. Honest answer: unknown.

No source in Franklin's writings, letters, or almanacs. The internal evidence argues against him outright: the right to pursue happiness appears in the Declaration of Independence, not the Constitution, and Franklin, a signer of both, would be an unlikely person to confuse them. The line reads as a 20th-century American aphorism retrofitted onto Franklin, who is one of the heaviest misattribution magnets in the corpus alongside Twain and Lincoln. I cannot identify an actual originator, hence apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Poor Richard's Almanack, Benjamin Franklin, 1746; reprinted in 'The Way to Wealth,' 1758
results.notes: Genuine Franklin. The correct wording is 'Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of' — the input's 'Does thou' is a transcription error and should be corrected to 'Dost thou' before the quote goes live. First published in Poor Richard's Almanack and later gathered into the preface essay 'The Way to Wealth' (1758).

Bennett W. Goodspeed was an investment writer best known for 'The Tao Jones Averages: A Guide to Whole-Brained Investing' (1983), a book built around exactly this kind of right-brain/left-brain aphorism, and my recollection associates the line with him. I cannot confirm the book or page with enough certainty to record a citation, so the print-source field stays null. Attribution plausible, source unconfirmed.

Bernie Siegel, the surgeon and author of 'Love, Medicine and Miracles' (1986) and 'Peace, Love and Healing,' is a plausible author and the sentiment is squarely within his body of work. I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and Siegel's material is heavily excerpted in devotional anthologies without citation, which is how unsourced attributions to him propagate. Credible but unverified.

The idea is genuinely Russell's but this exact wording is not sourced. The documented original is from his 1933 essay 'The Triumph of Stupidity': 'The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.' Several loose paraphrases circulate, including the popular 'the whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts,' which Wikiquote carries as unsourced. The text here ('the biggest cause of trouble... stupid people... intelligent folks') is another such variant, with an American register that does not sound like Russell. Recommend replacing with the sourced 1933 wording if this quote is wanted in the corpus.

Betty Eadie is the author of 'Embraced by the Light' (1992) and 'The Awakening Heart.' The passage's shift into second-person reflective prompts mid-paragraph suggests a devotional or workbook context rather than her narrative memoir, and it may be a compiler's stitching of separate lines. I cannot place it in a specific title. Also note the stray closing double-quote at the end of the text, which should be cleaned before publication.

The Betty Reese credit is the conventional one in quote books from roughly the 1980s onward, where she is usually identified only as an American public relations executive — an unusually thin biographical trail for an attribution. The mosquito image belongs to a larger family of sayings, including the widely circulated 'if you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito,' which is variously credited to the Dalai Lama and to an African proverb, none of them with a solid primary source. Attribution exists but is weak.

Consistently and long attributed to Bill Cosby, who is generally reported to have said it in interviews; the attribution is stable and I am not aware of any competing claimant or earlier appearance, which is why this sits above the pure-unverified tier. But I cannot name the interview, book, or date, so it falls short of the 0.80 promotion bar. Separate from provenance, the corpus owner may want to consider whether Cosby attributions belong in an inspirational collection at all.

Ubiquitous in leadership training material and consistently credited to Gates, usually with a vague pointer to a late-1990s speech, but I cannot name the occasion or a printed text. The 'next century' framing places the origin plausibly in the 1990s, which is consistent with the attribution without confirming it. Widely repeated is not the same as sourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Lady Sings the Blues, Billie Holiday with William Dufty, 1956 (as commonly cited; I cannot confirm the page)
results.notes: My recollection places this line in Holiday's autobiography 'Lady Sings the Blues,' and the imagery — white satin, gardenias, the plantation — is characteristic of that book's account of touring as a Black singer with white bands. Two caveats keep it below the promotion bar: I cannot confirm the page or chapter, and the book was ghostwritten by William Dufty, with scholars (notably Farah Jasmine Griffin and John Szwed) documenting that substantial parts of it are unreliable or not in Holiday's own words. The sentiment is authentically hers; the exact authorship of the sentence is shared with Dufty.

The circle teaching is authentically Black Elk's, but this terse six-word phrasing does not match the known texts. The famous passage in 'Black Elk Speaks' (John G. Neihardt, 1932) runs 'Everything the Power of the World does is done in a circle,' continuing through the round sky, the round sun and moon, and the whirling wind; 'The Sacred Pipe' (Joseph Epes Brown, 1953) develops the same idea. 'Everything sacred moves in a Circle' appears to be a condensation that circulates without a source. Additional caveat: both books are non-Lakota interlocutors' renderings of Black Elk's words, so even the canonical wordings are mediated. Recommend replacing with the sourced Neihardt line if this idea is wanted.

results.earliest_print_source: Pensées, Blaise Pascal, 1670 (fragment 139 Brunschvicg / 136 Lafuma)
results.notes: Genuine Pascal. French original: 'tout le malheur des hommes vient d'une seule chose, qui est de ne savoir pas demeurer en repos dans une chambre.' The English wording here is one of several standard translations ('All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone' is the other common rendering). Attribution is not in doubt; only the translation varies.

Consistent with Brian Greene's voice and subject matter, and I recall it circulating from 'The Elegant Universe' (1999), in the discussion of how relativity forces us to give up intuitions about space and time. I cannot place the chapter or page with enough certainty to cite it, so the print source is left null rather than guessed. No competing attribution exists, which supports the author even without a located source.

Brian Tracy is a real motivational author whose seminars and books (e.g. 'Maximum Achievement', 'Goals!') repeat this theme, and the attribution is consistent across quote aggregators. But the passage reads like transcribed seminar speech and I cannot place it in a specific book, article, or recorded talk. Plausible but unsourced; no competing attribution.

Widely and consistently attributed to Brian Tracy across quote collections and his own promotional material, with no rival claimant I know of. However the maxim belongs to a large family of older success-literature sayings about 'going the extra mile' (Napoleon Hill and Elbert Hubbard both worked this ground), so an earlier ancestor is possible. No specific book or talk locatable.

The line is much older than Brian Tracy. The known original is Elizabeth Bibesco (1897-1945, daughter of H. H. Asquith): 'Blessed are those who can give without remembering and take without forgetting.' It appears in her posthumous collection 'Haven' (1951) and is standardly attributed to her. Tracy and other motivational speakers quote it, which is how his name became attached. I am confident about Bibesco as the source of the saying but am not citing a page, so the print field is null.

I cannot place this in any authenticated Bruce Lee material ('Tao of Jeet Kune Do', 'Striking Thoughts', 'Artist of Life', or the interview record). It reads as a reworded version of the well-known aphorism 'Change is inevitable; growth is optional,' which is generally attributed to John C. Maxwell. Because the wording here differs materially and I cannot confirm the derivation chain, I am not asserting a reattribution. Bruce Lee is a moderate misattribution magnet: his notebooks copied maxims from mid-century self-help writers, and quote sites then credit him for them.

Genuinely Bruce Lee in substance. The 'be like water' teaching is documented on film in two 1971 sources: the Pierre Berton Show interview (December 1971) and the Longstreet episode 'The Way of the Intercepting Fist,' which carries the famous 'Be water, my friend.' The exact sentence quoted here appears to be a compressed/merged rendering of that spoken material rather than a verbatim line from a single source, so I am withholding a specific citation. Author attribution is safe; wording is approximate.

This is Wendell Phillips, the American abolitionist orator: 'What is defeat? Nothing but education, nothing but the first step to something better.' It is a well-established Phillips line from his mid-19th-century speeches and appears in standard quotation dictionaries under his name. Bruce Lee transcribed passages from other writers into his personal notebooks, and posthumous compilations plus quote sites have credited several such borrowings to him. Confident in Phillips as the originator.

Circulates under Bruce Lee's name but I cannot place it in his authenticated writings, and the phrasing is pure mid-century American positive-thinking literature (Napoleon Hill / Norman Vincent Peale register). Lee read and copied from those authors, so this may be another borrowed maxim recorded in his notebooks. I do not have a specific prior source, so no reattribution is asserted.

Among the better-supported Bruce Lee lines. I recall it from his own written notes as collected in the John Little-edited volumes, most likely 'Striking Thoughts: Bruce Lee's Wisdom for Daily Living' (2000). I am confident enough in Lee's authorship to call it attributed, but not confident enough about the exact volume and page to enter a print citation, so that field is null.

The widely circulated form is 'The successful warrior is the average man, with laser-like focus'; this entry is a de-gendered variant of that. I cannot locate either form in Bruce Lee's authenticated writings or interviews, and 'laser-like focus' is a late-20th-century business-motivation idiom rather than Lee's vocabulary. Probably a modern coinage that acquired his name. No alternative originator known.

Bruno Gröning (1906-1959) was a German faith healer, and this sentiment matches the teaching material published by the Bruno Gröning Circle of Friends, which is essentially the only body that transmits his sayings. That transmission is devotional and post-hoc rather than documentary, and I know of no contemporaneous published text or recording I could point to for this line. The attribution is plausible within that tradition but unverifiable from what I know.

Authentic Fuller vocabulary and syntax; in his own usage the subject is 'the comprehensive designer,' described as an emerging synthesis of artist, inventor, mechanic, objective economist and evolutionary strategist. My recall places it in 'Ideas and Integrities: A Spontaneous Autobiographical Disclosure' (1963), where the comprehensive designer is his central figure, but I am not certain enough to enter that as the citation. Author attribution is solid; the quoted version has been trimmed from 'comprehensive designer' to 'designer.'

results.earliest_print_source: Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, R. Buckminster Fuller, 1969
results.notes: Core Fuller, and the 'Spaceship Earth' framing plus the closing 'It has to be everybody or nobody' are both signature formulations of his from this period. I place the passage in 'Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth' (1969); Fuller also repeated the 'everybody or nobody' line in later lectures and in 'Critical Path' (1981), so the exact wording here may reflect one of those restatements rather than the 1969 text verbatim.

results.earliest_print_source: I Seem To Be A Verb, R. Buckminster Fuller, 1970
results.notes: This is Fuller's best-known self-description and it gave the 1970 book its title. The passage is reproduced widely from that source and is not contested. Confidence held at 0.85 rather than higher only because Fuller recycled the formulation across talks and books and I cannot confirm which appearance is earliest.

Not canonical Buddhism. This is a member of the 'watch your thoughts, they become words' family of sayings, which has been variously credited to the Buddha, Lao Tzu, Gandhi, and Margaret Thatcher, and whose traceable modern ancestors are the 'sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny' formula (attributed in the 19th century to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles) and a 1977 newspaper version credited to Frank Outlaw. None of these is Buddhist. I cannot identify which specific link in that chain produced this wording, so no reattribution is asserted.

results.earliest_print_source: The Dhammapada: The Sayings of the Buddha, trans. Thomas Byrom, 1976 (verses 1-2)
results.notes: This is Dhammapada 1-2 (Yamakavagga) in Thomas Byrom's 1976 rendering, which is the source of the familiar 'We are what we think' opening. Byrom is a free poetic translator: more literal versions render the opening as 'Mind precedes all mental states; mind is their chief.' So the underlying text is canonical and the ox-cart and shadow similes are genuine, but the English is Byrom's interpretation rather than a close translation. Attribution to 'Buddha' is correct in the traditional sense.

Not canonical. My recall places this in Jack Kornfield's 'Buddha's Little Instruction Book' (1994), a collection of Kornfield's own modern distillations written in the Buddha's voice, which is the documented origin of a whole cluster of pseudo-Buddha quotes now in circulation. The generic label 'Buddhist saying' is not false in spirit, but the line is a contemporary Western teacher's composition rather than a traditional saying. Reattribution offered with moderate rather than high confidence.

The input's own label is the honest one: this is a paraphrase, not a translation. The Kalama Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.65) is genuine canon and does urge the Kalamas not to accept teachings merely on the grounds of report, tradition, hearsay, scripture, logic, or a teacher's authority. But this English wording is a loose 19th/20th-century Western rendering of unknown authorship, and its final clause ('believe only what you yourself judge to be true') distorts the sutta, which asks the listener to test claims against whether they lead to harm or benefit and to weigh the judgment of the wise, not to make private judgment the sole criterion. Canonical basis real; this specific text unsourced and tendentious.

I can find no canonical or traditional Buddhist basis for this in what I know, and the aphorism's shape - an epigram about exploration and rarity - belongs to modern inspirational writing rather than to Pali or Mahayana sources. Origin unknown; the 'Buddhist saying' label appears to be decorative.

There is a genuine Buddhist antecedent for the candle image: the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters uses the simile of a torch from which many torches are lit without the original's light being diminished, applied to rejoicing in another's giving. So the first sentence has real textual ancestry. The second sentence, 'Happiness never decreases by being shared,' is a modern English addition, and the combined form circulating under the Buddha's name is not a translation of any single canonical passage. Genuine root, modern composite wording.

Doctrinally unobjectionable - samadhi as the proximate cause of panna is standard Theravada teaching, and Dhammapada 282 says meditation gives rise to wisdom - but I cannot match this seven-word sentence to any canonical verse or standard translation. It reads as a modern summary of the threefold training rather than a quotation. Sentiment traditional, wording unsourced.

This is a recognisable paraphrase of Udana 8.3 (the Nibbana Sutta): 'There is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned. If there were not, there would be no escape from the born, become, made, conditioned.' The canonical source is secure, so the Buddhist attribution is sound, but the sentence as quoted matches no standard translation I know - it converts the sutta's existence claim into a claim about seeing and being liberated. Cited as a paraphrase, not a translation; no print citation entered because I cannot identify which populariser produced this wording.

The threefold structure is canonical - Anguttara Nikaya teaches that the giver's mind is gladdened before giving, during giving, and on recollecting the gift afterwards. But this English passage is modern expository prose, not a translation, and its register suggests a contemporary Western vipassana teacher (Sharon Salzberg's 'Lovingkindness' and Joseph Goldstein's writing both cover this ground). I cannot confirm which, so I am naming no author. Doctrine authentic, wording modern and unattributed.

The phrase long predates Byron Katie in its plural form: June Jordan's 'Poem for South African Women' (1978) gives 'we are the ones we have been waiting for,' later popularised via the Hopi elders' prophecy and Alice Walker's 2006 book title. The singular form used here is also the title of Richard Schwartz's Internal Family Systems book 'You Are the One You've Been Waiting For' (2008). Byron Katie may well say it in her workshops - it fits The Work - but I cannot confirm she originated it or place it in her books, and the earlier uses make an exclusive attribution to her unsafe. No reattribution asserted because I cannot establish who coined the singular form.

Consistent with Byron Katie's idiom and with themes in 'Loving What Is' (2002) and 'A Thousand Names for Joy' (2007), but I cannot place this exact sentence in any of her books, transcripts, or interviews I know. Her published lines on this theme run closer to 'I am the only one who can love me' and 'When the mind is loved, there is nothing left to seek.' Treat the wording as unsourced paraphrase until someone checks a primary text.

Byron Katie does speak of heaven and hell as functions of believed thoughts ('When I believe my thoughts, I suffer; when I don't, I don't'), so the sentiment is squarely hers. But I cannot locate this precise formulation in a specific book or recorded event. Most likely a transcribed remark from an event or an approximate rendering. No primary citation available from my knowledge.

This is one of Byron Katie's genuine signature phrases — she uses it repeatedly in The Work events and in her writing to point at the absence of separation between self and other. Attribution to her is consistent and I have no competing claimant. Held below the promotion bar only because I cannot name a specific book and page; 'A Thousand Names for Joy' (2007) is the likeliest home but I am not confirming it.

Katie's documented formulations run 'The world is nothing but my perception of it' and 'I am the world I perceive.' This variant reads like a compressed retelling of that idea rather than a sentence I can match to a source. Attribution to Katie is plausible; the wording is unverified.

Generic enough that it could come from many contemplative teachers. I cannot place it in Byron Katie's published work, and nothing in the phrasing is distinctively hers. No traceable source in my knowledge; honest answer is 'I don't know.'

Two problems. First, the popular phrasing traces to the Lewis CHARACTER in William Nicholson's 'Shadowlands' (stage play 1989, film 1993), where Anthony Hopkins as Lewis says roughly 'I pray because I can't help myself... It doesn't change God, it changes me.' That is Nicholson's dialogue, not Lewis's prose. Second, the underlying aphorism is much older and is solidly Kierkegaard's: 'Prayer does not change God, but it changes him who prays.' Lewis wrote at length on petitionary prayer in 'Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer' (1964) but I know of no passage there matching this sentence. Confidence value reflects the weak attribution to Lewis; I hold the misattribution verdict itself with reasonable certainty.
results.suggested_reattribution: William Nicholson (Shadowlands screenplay, 1993) for this phrasing; Søren Kierkegaard for the underlying aphorism

results.notes: C. West Churchman, the systems scientist, made questioning of foundational assumptions the core of his method, and this line circulates in systems-thinking and operations-research literature attributed to him. 'The Systems Approach' (1968) and 'Challenge to Reason' (1968) are the plausible homes, but I cannot confirm which book or page, so I am not asserting a print source. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; the citation is missing.

Widely and consistently attributed to Albert Camus, and a French original circulates ('On ne vous pardonne votre bonheur et vos succès que si vous consentez généreusement à les partager'), which is a good sign of genuine provenance rather than an English-only invention. I cannot confirm the work — candidates include the Carnets and the essays of 'L'Été' — so no print source is asserted. Note also that the corpus record's author field is the bare surname 'Camus' and the context field reads 'Philosopher, Architect,' which looks like a data error worth fixing regardless of the provenance verdict.

Consistently attributed to Camus with a circulating French original ('Il n'y a que le malheur à n'être pas aimé: il y a la misère à ne point aimer'), and the malheur/misère distinction is characteristically his. I believe it comes from the Carnets or an early essay, but I cannot confirm the work, so no print source is claimed. Same data note as q_0407: author is recorded as bare 'Camus' with a 'Philosopher, Architect' context string.

This is the internet's favourite Jung line and it is a paraphrase, not his sentence. The documented original is from 'Aion' (1951), CW 9ii, para. 126: 'When an inner situation is not made conscious, it appears outside as fate.' The 'until you make the unconscious conscious... and you will call it fate' rendering has no located primary text and is generally listed among Jung's unsourced or paraphrased attributions. The idea is genuinely his; the wording is not. Consider replacing with the Aion sentence, which is citable.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Stages of Life" (1930-31), in Modern Man in Search of a Soul, Carl Jung, 1933; Collected Works vol. 8, para. 784
results.notes: Genuine Jung from the essay 'The Stages of Life,' delivered as a lecture around 1930 and collected in 'Modern Man in Search of a Soul' (English translation 1933); it also appears in CW 8, 'The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche.' Standard translation reads '...for what was great in the morning will be little at evening, and what in the morning was true will at evening have become a lie.' The version here is a slightly trimmed rendering of that passage but faithful to it.

results.earliest_print_source: Commentary on "The Secret of the Golden Flower" (1929), Carl Jung; Collected Works vol. 13, para. 18
results.notes: Genuine Jung, from his commentary on Richard Wilhelm's translation of 'The Secret of the Golden Flower' (1929), reprinted in CW 13, 'Alchemical Studies.' The quoted text is a lightly modernized rendering — Hull's translation has 'outgrowing' rather than 'outgrowth,' 'arose on the person's horizon' rather than 'appeared,' 'life-tendency' rather than 'life urge,' and does not contain 'his or her.' Source and substance are solid; the exact wording has drifted, so a copy-editor may want to restore the Hull text.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Philosophical Tree" (1945, revised 1954), Carl Jung; Collected Works vol. 13, para. 335
results.notes: Genuine and correctly worded. From Jung's essay 'The Philosophical Tree,' collected in CW 13, 'Alchemical Studies.' One of the few widely circulated Jung shadow-work quotes that survives checking against the primary text intact.

results.earliest_print_source: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, Carl Jung (recorded and edited by Aniela Jaffé), 1961/1963
results.notes: Genuine, from the late chapter on life after death in 'Memories, Dreams, Reflections' (German 1962, English translation 1963). Wording as quoted matches the Winston translation. Worth noting for the corpus that MDR is a collaboratively edited memoir rather than a work Jung wrote start to finish, but this passage is attributed to him directly.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Fanny Bowditch, 22 October 1916, in C. G. Jung Letters, Vol. 1: 1906-1950 (Princeton/Bollingen, 1973)
results.notes: Genuine, from a letter Jung wrote to his former analysand Fanny Bowditch in October 1916, published in the first volume of the Bollingen 'Letters.' Both sentences belong together in the original, which is unusual — most viral Jung couplets are stitched from two places. The line is sometimes challenged online, but the letter source is real and citable.

The sentiment is consistent with Jung's late thinking on the psyche's continuity with the world (the unus mundus and synchronicity material), so attribution is plausible. But I cannot place this sentence in the Collected Works, the letters, or the seminars, and I am not going to guess a volume. Unverified wording.

One of the most-repeated Sagan lines and one of the least sourced. It does not appear in Cosmos, The Demon-Haunted World, Pale Blue Dot, or Broca's Brain as far as I know, and it is generally listed among Sagan's unsourced or disputed attributions rather than in the sourced sections. Sagan may well have said something like it in an interview, but no primary citation exists in my knowledge. Do not promote. Note also that this quote is duplicated in this batch as q_0418.

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995
results.notes: Genuine Sagan from 'The Demon-Haunted World' (1995), in the opening material where he sets out why he prefers reality to consolation. Wording matches the published text. This is one of his best-attested lines.

Exact duplicate of q_0416 (same text, same author; only the category field differs — q_0416 has a null category). Same verdict: widely circulated, no located primary source in any Sagan book or documented broadcast, generally treated as unsourced. Recommend deduplicating these two records regardless of the provenance decision.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, episode 9, "The Lives of the Stars" (PBS, 1980); also Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Random House, 1980
results.notes: Genuine and precisely worded. Sagan says it in episode 9 of the 1980 television series while making an apple pie, and the line appears in the companion book. About as well-documented as a Sagan quote gets.

Sagan definitely wrote and said a passage of this kind — the well-documented version is from Cosmos, 'The Persistence of Memory' (episode 11 and the corresponding book chapter): 'What an astonishing thing a book is... One glance at it and you're inside the mind of another person, maybe somebody dead for thousands of years.' The compressed phrasing here, ending 'To read is to voyage through time,' is close to but not identical with that text, and it may instead come from his later writing on literacy in 'The Demon-Haunted World.' Author attribution is safe; the exact wording and source are not pinned, so I am not asserting a print citation. Someone should check the Cosmos chapter and align the wording before promotion.

The Frederick Douglass and literacy material is genuinely Sagan's territory — 'The Demon-Haunted World' (1995) devotes a chapter to Douglass teaching himself to read and to literacy as liberation, which is the near-certain home of this passage. I cannot confirm the exact sentence or page, so no print source is asserted. Separately, the corpus text misspells the name: it should be Frederick Douglass with two s's. Fix that before any promotion.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, episode 1, "The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean" (PBS, 1980); also Cosmos, Carl Sagan, Random House, 1980
results.notes: Genuine and accurately quoted, including the 'star stuff' coinage that became Sagan's signature. Delivered in the first episode of the 1980 series and printed in the companion book. Strongest possible attribution short of a manuscript.

results.earliest_print_source: The Cosmic Connection: An Extraterrestrial Perspective, Carl Sagan, Anchor Press/Doubleday, 1973
results.notes: Genuine Sagan from 'The Cosmic Connection' (1973), in the material on interspecies and interstellar communication, where the dolphin example serves his point about human parochialism in imagining contact. Wording and dry cadence match the published text. Slightly below 0.9 only because I am recalling the book rather than a specific page.

results.earliest_print_source: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, Carl Sagan, Random House, 1994, chapter 1
results.notes: Genuine — the central portion of the 'Pale Blue Dot' reflection on the 1990 Voyager 1 photograph, from the opening chapter of the 1994 book, and later widely circulated as a recorded reading. This excerpt begins mid-passage; the full text opens 'Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us.' Two mechanical notes for the corpus: the double hyphens should be em dashes, and given the length this is arguably a passage rather than a quote — consider whether it wants an excerpt marker.

results.earliest_print_source: Contact, Carl Sagan, 1985 (dedication to Ann Druyan)
results.notes: This is the dedication line of Sagan's novel Contact (Simon & Schuster, 1985), addressed to Ann Druyan. I recall it as printed dedication text rather than narrative prose, and the wording circulates unchanged. Strong, stable attribution.

Consistently attributed to Sagan, usually to Cosmos (1980), and consistent with his voice. My hesitation: it is suspiciously close to the better-documented line 'We can judge our progress by the courage of our questions and the depth of our answers...' (see q_0432), and one may be a circulated compression of the other. I cannot place this exact sentence at a specific page or chapter from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing at Cosmos.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 12 ('Encyclopaedia Galactica')
results.notes: I recall this passage from the Cosmos book, in the discussion of what a cosmic perspective implies for how we treat one another. The three-sentence structure and the 'hundred billion galaxies' figure are Sagan's own and match the book's text as I know it.

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995, ch. 2 ('Science and Hope')
results.notes: A well-documented passage from The Demon-Haunted World. The full paragraph — including the Gandhi and King examples and the closing 'does a disservice to both' — matches the book text as I know it. This is one of the most reliably sourced Sagan quotations on science and spirituality.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 11 ('The Persistence of Memory')
results.notes: The 'a book is made from a tree' passage is from the Cosmos chapter on memory, writing, and libraries. Wording matches what I know of the book. Note a stray trailing double-quote character at the end of the stored text that should be cleaned before publication.

The idea is genuinely Sagan's, but this exact wording appears to be a popular condensation. The documented Cosmos (1980, ch. 13) phrasings I know are 'starstuff pondering the stars' and 'We are star stuff which has taken its destiny into its own hands'; Cosmos also has 'We are star stuff harvesting starlight.' 'Star-stuff contemplating the stars' reads like a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation. Not a misattribution to another author — a wording problem. Recommend replacing with a documented variant if the corpus wants an exact quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 11 ('The Persistence of Memory')
results.notes: The library passage comes from the same Cosmos chapter as the 'a book is made from a tree' text (q_0429). The two are near neighbors in the book. Wording matches my recollection of the printed text.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980 (Introduction)
results.notes: I recall this sentence from the front matter of Cosmos, where Sagan sets out the book's stance toward evidence. The 'willingness to embrace what is true rather than what feels good' clause is distinctive and I am confident it is Sagan's own text rather than a paraphrase. Chapter placement (Introduction) is my recollection and slightly less certain than the authorship.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Wonder and Skepticism', Carl Sagan, Skeptical Inquirer 19(1), January/February 1995
results.notes: I recall this passage from Sagan's 'Wonder and Skepticism' — the keynote he gave to CSICOP, published in Skeptical Inquirer in early 1995. The '400 billion other stars' figure and the closing 'well worth pondering' are characteristic of that piece. Confident in Sagan's authorship; moderately confident in this specific venue as the earliest print appearance.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980 (Introduction)
results.notes: This is the opening of the Introduction to Cosmos — 'Lost somewhere between immensity and eternity is our tiny planetary home' through 'a mote of dust in the morning sky.' Long, distinctive, and stably reproduced; I am confident in both the author and the placement.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980 (chapter unconfirmed)
results.notes: Confident this is authentic Sagan prose — the cadence, the framing of superstition as avoidance, and 'the weave and structure of the Cosmos' are all his. Less confident about the locus: it is generally cited to Cosmos (1980), but I cannot rule out Broca's Brain (1979), which covers similar ground. Recording the book with an explicit caveat rather than inventing a chapter.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 12 ('Encyclopaedia Galactica')
results.notes: The 'built-in, error-correcting machinery' passage is from Cosmos, in the chapter dealing with science, civilizations, and the survival of intelligence. The self-deprecating aside ('Some may consider this an overbroad characterization') is a Sagan hallmark and matches the printed text as I know it.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 13 ('Who Speaks for Earth?')
results.notes: From the closing chapter of Cosmos, in the passage beginning 'We are the local embodiment of a Cosmos grown to self-awareness.' Also spoken in the Cosmos television series (1980). One of the best-documented Sagan lines.

This is film dialogue, not Sagan's writing. It is spoken by the extraterrestrial (appearing as Ellie's father) in the 1997 Warner Bros. film Contact, whose screenplay was written by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. Sagan and Ann Druyan wrote the original story on which the film was based, and Sagan died in December 1996 before its release, but I do not believe this speech appears in Sagan's 1985 novel. Attributing it to Sagan as an author is not supportable; it belongs to the screenwriters.
results.suggested_reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995, ch. 2 ('Science and Hope')
results.notes: I recall this sentence from The Demon-Haunted World, in the discussion of why nature repeatedly outruns human intuition. The leading 'But' indicates it has been lifted mid-paragraph; the corpus may want to drop it. Confident in author and book, slightly less so in the exact chapter.

Widely and consistently attributed to Sagan, commonly to Cosmos (1980) and to the television series. It is short and aphoristic, which is exactly the shape of quotation that drifts, and I cannot place it at a specific page from memory. Nothing suggests another author — this is uncertainty about sourcing, not about attribution. Below the promotion bar on locus alone.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 9 ('The Lives of the Stars')
results.notes: From the Cosmos chapter on stellar nucleosynthesis and atomic structure, in the passage on cutting an apple pie down to its atoms. The two-sentence form matches the printed text as I know it. Confident in the book; chapter attribution is my recollection.

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995
results.notes: The 'winnowed from deep nonsense' formulation is from The Demon-Haunted World, in Sagan's argument that skepticism serves religion as well as science. I am confident in the book and the wording; I cannot pin the chapter, and a variant of the thought also appears in his 1987 CSICOP talk 'The Burden of Skepticism.'

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995 (chapter on patriotism and dissent, 'Real Patriots Ask Questions')
results.notes: I recall this passage from the late chapters of The Demon-Haunted World, where Sagan argues that a democracy needs citizens trained in skeptical inquiry and that dissent is a national asset. Confident in the book; the chapter title is my best recollection and is offered with that caveat.

results.earliest_print_source: Broca's Brain: Reflections on the Romance of Science, Carl Sagan, 1979 (chapter unconfirmed)
results.notes: Unmistakably Sagan's prose — the catalogue structure ('quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies') and the closing turn on 'the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience' are his. My recollection places it in Broca's Brain, most likely the pseudoscience essay 'Night Walkers and Mystery Mongers,' but I hold that loosely; it could belong to Cosmos or The Demon-Haunted World, which cover the same terrain. Author confident, locus uncertain.

The creativity/skepticism tension is one of Sagan's signature arguments — most fully developed in 'The Burden of Skepticism' (Skeptical Inquirer, 1987) and in the introduction to Broca's Brain (1979), where he writes of an 'exquisite balance' between the two. This particular sentence is consistently attributed to him and fits, but I cannot confidently assign it to either source, so I am leaving the print citation null rather than picking one.

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 1 ('The Shores of the Cosmic Ocean')
results.notes: The opening lines of Cosmos, also the opening narration of the television series. 'The Cosmos is all that is or ever was or ever will be' is among the most securely documented sentences Sagan wrote. Minor note: the canonical wording is 'all that is or ever was or ever will be' — the stored text drops the first 'ever.'

To my knowledge this is dialogue from the 1997 film Contact — spoken by Ted Arroway to young Ellie and echoed by her later — and not text Sagan wrote. I recall it being listed among misattributions on Sagan's Wikiquote page for exactly this reason. Sagan wrote the novel and co-wrote the story, so the association is understandable, but the screenplay is by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. I am not certain the line is absent from the 1985 novel, which is why this is 'likely' rather than settled; a text search of the novel would resolve it.
results.suggested_reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

results.earliest_print_source: Cosmos, Carl Sagan, 1980, ch. 13 ('Who Speaks for Earth?')
results.notes: I recall the 'arrogant newcomer' passage from the closing chapter of Cosmos, in Sagan's argument that no existing institution has a monopoly on answers for human survival. The 'four and a half billion years of other acts' image and the closing 'our task is to find them' match my recollection of the printed text.

results.earliest_print_source: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, Carl Sagan, 1994 (chapter unconfirmed)
results.notes: This is the opening of a longer Sagan passage that continues 'It matters what those visions are. Often they become self-fulfilling prophecies. Dreams are maps.' My recollection places it in Pale Blue Dot, but I cannot confirm the chapter and cannot rule out one of his Parade essays from the same period. Author attribution is solid; the citation is offered with an explicit caveat. Note also that the single-sentence excerpt is weaker than the full passage.

results.earliest_print_source: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, Carl Sagan, 1995
results.notes: Genuine Sagan, from Chapter 2 ('Science and Hope') of The Demon-Haunted World (1995). The line continues '...When we recognize our place in an immensity of light-years and in the passage of ages...' Wording in the corpus matches the published sentence exactly.

Consistently attributed to Carl Sandburg across quotation collections and never, to my knowledge, to anyone else, which is mild evidence for authenticity. I cannot place it in a specific poem, essay, or interview, and I have no recollection of a primary citation. Attribution is stable but unverified at the source level.

Carlo Carretto (1910-1988), Little Brother of Jesus, is the consistent attribution and the passage matches his devotional style and his repeated 'Love, and...' constructions. Most likely from Letters from the Desert (Lettere dal deserto, 1964) or The God Who Comes, but I cannot confirm which book or verify the English translation wording, so no print source is asserted.

Reads as a don Juan teaching from the Castaneda corpus and the vocabulary ('warrior', 'ordinary man', 'challenge') is characteristic of Tales of Power (1974) and the aphorism compilation The Wheel of Time (1998). I cannot pin the volume or page. Separate caveat for the corpus: Castaneda's don Juan material is widely held by scholars to be fiction, so 'Castaneda wrote it' is a different claim from 'a Yaqui teacher said it'.

The Fuentes attribution circulates in quotation aggregators but I cannot locate it in any of his novels, essays, or interviews from memory. The underlying idea ('cruelty is a failure of imagination') is a commonplace that has been voiced by several writers, which makes single-author attribution weak. Honest answer: unplaced.

Catherine Ponder, New Thought minister, is the uniform attribution and the phrasing ('bound to that person by an emotional link stronger than steel') matches her prosperity-and-forgiveness teaching. Probably from The Dynamic Laws of Prosperity (1962) or a companion Dynamic Laws title, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so no citation is asserted.

Attributed to Catherine the Great in English quotation dictionaries, but I know of no primary Russian or French source in her correspondence or memoirs. The sentiment closely tracks the older French maxim 'tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner' (associated with Mme de Stael, Corinne, 1807), and the line is also floated under Confucius, which is a classic sign of a free-floating aphorism. Attribution is plausible but unsupported.

Cavett Robert (1907-1997), founder of the National Speakers Association, is the consistent attribution and the passage is idiomatic of mid-century American motivational speaking, so authorship is plausible. His material circulated largely through recorded talks rather than books, and I cannot cite a published source or a datable first appearance.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Lessons from Europe for American Business', Leon C. Megginson, Southwestern Social Science Quarterly, vol. 44, 1963
results.notes: Not Darwin. This is one of the best-documented misattributions in the corpus: it originates as Leon C. Megginson's 1963 paraphrase of ideas in On the Origin of Species ('...it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment...'). Later compression into a terse epigram, plus quotation marks, converted the paraphrase into a fake Darwin quote. Wikiquote lists it under Darwin's misattributed section. Darwin himself never wrote it; 'survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase, adopted by Darwin only in later editions.

Unlike q_0458 this one is generally treated as genuine Darwin and is usually said to come from his correspondence, plausibly by way of The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (ed. Francis Darwin, 1887). I cannot identify the specific letter, recipient, or date from memory, so I will not assert a citation. Given that Darwin is a misattribution magnet, moderate rather than high confidence is the honest reading.

Uniformly attributed to the French critic Charles du Bos (1882-1939), most likely from his Approximations essays or his Journal, and the aphoristic register fits him. I cannot confirm the French original or a volume, and the English wording varies ('at a moment's notice' / 'at any moment'), which suggests translation drift. No citation asserted.

Well established as Charles Eames and quoted throughout design literature and Eames Office material; it is one of the lines the Eames Office itself repeats. Circulates in two variants ('They make the design' and '...they make the product'), which indicates it comes from spoken remarks or interviews rather than a fixed printed text. Strong attribution, no single primary source I can cite.

Charles John Quarto is a real songwriter and poet, but I have no independent knowledge of this line in his published work. It appears to circulate only through quotation aggregators. No traceable source; 'I don't know' is the accurate verdict.

Genuine Swindoll in substance: this is from his much-anthologized 'Attitude' material, the same body of writing as the far more famous 'The longer I live, the more I realize the impact of attitude on life' passage. My recollection places it in Strengthening Your Grip (1982), in the chapter on attitudes, but I am not confident enough in the book or year to assert it as a citation. Note that Swindoll's attitude texts are heavily paraphrased online, so the exact wording here may not be his published wording.

Attributed to 'Charles Schwab' without disambiguation. Period and diction point to Charles M. Schwab (1862-1939) of Bethlehem Steel, not Charles R. Schwab the modern broker; if genuine it most likely comes from his popular business writing of the 1910s-20s, possibly Succeeding With What You Have (1917). I cannot confirm the source, and the ambiguity of the bare name is itself a provenance defect worth fixing in the corpus.
results.suggested_reattribution: Charles M. Schwab (Bethlehem Steel, 1862-1939) - disambiguation, not reattribution

results.notes: Almost certainly not Tecumseh. Tecumseh died in 1813 and his authenticated speeches survive only through interpreters and hostile or secondhand transcription; this polished English passage is not among them and has no contemporaneous record. Its wide circulation is modern - it spread through 20th-century 'Native American wisdom' anthologies and then explosively through the 2012 film Act of Valor, which used it as a closing text. The style (aphoristic, individualist, self-help cadence) reads as 20th-century composition. I cannot identify the actual author, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. Recommend not promoting it under a named historical figure.

This is a genuine Chinese proverb rather than a floating Western invention: it renders the common saying bu pa man, jiu pa zhan (不怕慢，就怕站), 'do not fear going slow, fear only standing still'. The corpus text says 'changing slowly' where the standard English rendering is 'growing slowly' - a variant, not a different proverb. Confidence reflects that the genre label 'Chinese proverb' is accurate; a proverb by nature has no single author or first printing.

Corresponds to the widely used Chinese saying ren yi shi zhi qi, mian bai ri zhi you (忍一时之气，免百日之忧), 'endure a moment's anger, avoid a hundred days of sorrow'. The label 'Chinese proverb' is therefore accurate as a genre attribution. As with all proverbs there is no author and no first-print source to verify.

The 'Chinese proverb' label is doubtful. The thought is Chan/Zen rather than proverbial - closest classical antecedent is Layman Pang's 'my miraculous power and spiritual activity: drawing water and carrying firewood'. The specific modern English phrasing most resembles Thich Nhat Hanh's line 'The miracle is not to walk on water; the miracle is to walk on the green earth', which is Vietnamese Zen, not a Chinese proverb. I am not confident enough to name a true source, so no reattribution is suggested, but the current label should be treated as unreliable.

A much-laundered saying: variously credited to Confucius, Xunzi, Benjamin Franklin, Native American sources, and 'Chinese proverb', which is the signature of an aphorism with no real home. There is a genuine classical antecedent in the Xunzi (ch. 8): hearing is not as good as seeing, seeing is not as good as knowing, knowing is not as good as putting into practice - but the modern tell/show/involve triad appears to be a 20th-century Western educational formulation rather than a translation. Label is unreliable; true origin unidentified.

Circulates as both a Chinese proverb and as a line by Hada Bejar, and neither attribution has support I can verify. I know of no Chinese original for it, which weakens the proverb label. Untraceable from training knowledge.

Christina Baldwin is the consistent attribution and the passage matches her journal-writing and spiritual-practice books, most likely Life's Companion: Journal Writing as a Spiritual Quest (1990). I cannot confirm the book or page. Note also that the corpus text is elided with an ellipsis, so it splices two non-adjacent sentences - worth flagging independent of authorship.

I have no knowledge of Christopher LaBrec as a published author or public figure, and no recollection of this line outside quotation aggregators. It has the shape of a motivational-poster attribution of unknown origin. Honest verdict: unverifiable.

Clarence Francis, chairman of General Foods (1935-1954), is the standard and stable attribution in management literature, typically credited to a speech or company address in the 1940s-50s. I cannot name the speech or date. The corpus text is gender-neutralized ('a person's time... their physical presence'); the circulating original reads 'a man's time... his physical presence', which should be noted if the quote is promoted.

Genuine Clarissa Pinkola Estes. This passage is from her widely circulated essay known as 'We Were Made for These Times' / 'Letter to a Young Activist During Troubled Times', which spread online in the early 2000s and was later collected in her published work. I am confident about the essay but not about its first print appearance or exact date, so no citation is asserted. Caveat: the online versions of this essay vary in wording and are sometimes reordered, so the exact text here may be a circulated variant.

A staple of Native American oratory anthologies, consistently attributed to Cochise and plausibly drawn from accounts of his 1871-72 negotiations with U.S. officers (the Howard/Jeffords parleys). I cannot confirm an original transcript or the anthology that first printed it. All surviving Cochise speech is mediated through interpreters and later journalistic reconstruction, so even a genuine source would be a secondhand rendering. Honest answer: plausible, unconfirmed.

Does not appear in the Analects or any Confucian classic that I know of. This is a modern English-language aphorism that spread through 20th-century quotation books and later quote sites; the tidy 'noblest / easiest / bitterest' rhetorical triad is characteristic of Western epigram construction, not of the Analects' terse recorded exchanges. I do not know who actually composed it, so I offer no reattribution. Confucius is a magnet for invented maxims of exactly this shape.

results.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 (Text)
results.notes: The antithesis 'host to God or hostage to the ego' is genuine ACIM language and recurs in the Text; I am confident of the source work but not of the exact chapter/section, so I have not cited one. The line as given here is phrased as a question and reads as a rewording of the canonical declarative sentence rather than a verbatim quotation, which is why this is 'attributed' rather than 'verified'. Anyone promoting this should check the wording against the FIP Text.

Consistently attributed to Cyrus H. K. Curtis, the Curtis Publishing / Saturday Evening Post publisher, in mid-20th-century business-epigram collections of the B. C. Forbes type. I cannot place a primary source — no speech, letter, or interview I can name — and business aphorisms of this vintage migrate freely between Curtis, Carnegie, and other publisher-industrialist figures. Plausible but unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: "Nottingham and the Mining Countryside", D. H. Lawrence, Architectural Review, 1930 (collected in Phoenix: The Posthumous Papers of D. H. Lawrence, 1936)
results.notes: Genuine Lawrence, from his late essay on the ugliness of the English mining towns. Note the wording: Lawrence wrote 'The human soul needs actual beauty even more than bread.' The corpus text drops 'even'. Recommend restoring the original word before promotion.

The content and idiom are consistent with D. T. Suzuki's expository writing on Zen (An Introduction to Zen Buddhism, Essays in Zen Buddhism, and the Barrett-edited Selected Writings), and the closing chain 'Nature is Mind, Mind is Buddha, Buddha is the Way, the Way is Zen' echoes the Chan formulations he liked to render in English. But I cannot place the volume or page, and the ellipsis suggests the line has been stitched from a longer passage. Note also that quote sites routinely confuse D. T. Suzuki with Shunryu Suzuki, so the attribution deserves a source check.

results.earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970
results.notes: This is Shunryu Suzuki, not D. T. Suzuki. The passage is from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind — the plainspoken lecture voice ('it won't help you through and through', 'without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything') is Shunryu Suzuki's transcribed dharma-talk register, not D. T. Suzuki's scholarly prose. My confidence in the reattribution to Shunryu Suzuki is high (~0.85); the 0.2 above reflects confidence in the stated author, D. T. Suzuki, which is low. I am confident of the book but not of the chapter, so none is cited. This is the single most common Suzuki/Suzuki mix-up in quote corpora.

results.earliest_print_source: The Sutra of Hui Neng (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch), trans. Wong Mou-lam, 1930 — Chapter 2, 'On Prajna'
results.notes: Genuine passage from the Platform Sutra in the Wong Mou-lam English translation, which is the source of nearly all quote-site Huineng. Two caveats: (1) authorship by Huineng himself is traditional rather than documentary — the text was compiled by disciples and grew across recensions; (2) the corpus line is slightly compressed against Wong's fuller sentence, which continues '...before we can know our own Essence of Mind.' The author name should be normalized: 'Daijan' is the posthumous title Dajian, so 'Dajian Huineng' or simply 'Huineng'.

Consistent with Ikeda's enormous published output of guidance essays, editorials, and daily-encouragement columns circulated through SGI publications, and I have no reason to doubt it. But that same output is the problem: his aphorisms circulate detached from the essay or speech they came from, and I cannot name the source. Plausible, unplaced.

Ubiquitous on quote sites under the Dalai Lama's name, but I can identify no book, talk, or interview behind it. The generic phrasing is typical of lines that accrete to him rather than originate with him. The 14th Dalai Lama is a strong misattribution magnet — the volume of translated, transcribed, and paraphrased teaching makes him easy to attach anything to.

This is Pema Chodron, not the Dalai Lama. The harden/soften antithesis closing on 'We always have the choice' is one of her signature passages, from her late-1990s/early-2000s books (When Things Fall Apart, 1997, and The Places That Scare You, 2001 are the two candidates I would check first) — I am confident of the author but not of which book, so I cite neither rather than guess. Confidence in the reattribution to Chodron is roughly 0.75; the 0.2 above reflects the stated attribution to the Dalai Lama.

One of the better-supported Dalai Lama attributions: it appears in edited collections of his teachings from around 1990 onward and is quoted with unusually stable wording, which usually indicates a real printed origin rather than internet drift. It also matches his repeated public formulation 'my religion is kindness.' I cannot name the specific volume or talk, so I leave the source null rather than guess at one. Strong secondary evidence, no primary source in hand.

The length, the qualified argument, and the human/animal contrast are characteristic of the Dalai Lama's book-length ethical writing of the late 1990s (Ethics for the New Millennium, The Art of Happiness with Howard Cutler) rather than of a fabricated aphorism — invented quotes are rarely this long or this hedged. That raises my confidence that it is genuine, but I cannot place the book or article, and passages of this kind are often lightly edited by whoever excerpts them.

Widely circulated under the Dalai Lama's name, often via daily-wisdom compilations of the Path to Tranquility type edited by Renuka Singh. The content matches his standard teaching against self-disparagement, which he treats as a distinctively Western affliction. No primary source I can name, and compilation books rarely cite their own origins, so the chain of custody is weak.

Reads as a composite: three separate Dalai Lama themes welded into one paragraph. 'Kindness is my true religion' is a real and characteristic formulation of his; the sentences on either side circulate independently elsewhere. Composite quotes are common on aggregator sites and are individually genuine but collectively unsourceable. I would not promote this as a single utterance without finding a source that carries all three sentences together.

Extremely famous and almost universally attributed to the Dalai Lama, but to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section on Wikiquote rather than the sourced section — no book, speech, or interview has been pinned to it. Fame is not evidence: this is a case where near-universal attribution coexists with zero documented provenance. Honest verdict is low confidence despite how well known the line is.

A near-ubiquitous Dalai Lama attribution with very stable wording, and it faithfully renders a real and repeated theme in his teaching on compassion as self-interested as well as altruistic. But I cannot locate a primary source, and like several of his most-shared lines it may be a compressed paraphrase of a longer spoken passage rather than a verbatim quotation.

Length and the first-person 'I am convinced' make a genuine spoken or written origin likely — this reads like transcript, not aggregator invention. Consistent with his talks and writings on compassion practice (The Compassionate Life and similar collections would be where I would look). No source I can name, so the attribution stays unverified.

'Warm heart' and 'warm-heartedness' are genuine signature terms of the Dalai Lama's public teaching, which supports the attribution at a thematic level. But the intelligence-plus-heart construction is also a widely shared moral commonplace — compare King's 'intelligence plus character' — and I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his talks or books. Thematically plausible, textually unplaced.

Contested and probably not Carnegie. This chiasmus circulates under several names — Dale Carnegie, Ingrid Bergman, and others — which is the classic signature of a floating aphorism that predates all of its claimed authors. I do not recall encountering it in How to Win Friends and Influence People or How to Stop Worrying and Start Living. Because I cannot identify a probable true origin, I am recording this as unverified rather than as a misattribution, but the Carnegie credit should be treated as weak.

Attributed to Dale E. Turner, the Seattle-area minister and long-running Seattle Times columnist, and the sentiment and cadence fit his inspirational column work. His columns are the likely origin, but individual columns are rarely cited by the quote collections that reprint him, and I cannot name a date or title. Plausible, unconfirmed.

Consistent with Dan Millman's vocabulary — 'conscious evolution', 'obstructions' — and with his post-Peaceful Warrior instructional books (No Ordinary Moments, The Life You Were Born to Live, The Laws of Spirit). Millman is a living author who circulates his own lines, so the attribution itself is low-risk, but I cannot name the book or page.

A recognizable Millman line with a distinctive image (backing up to get a running start) that argues against generic invention, and consistent with his 1990s books. Attribution to Millman is low-risk; the specific source is unplaced in my knowledge, so it stays unverified.

'Energy follows thought' is a New Thought commonplace that long predates Millman, but the surrounding sentences ('we move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine') are his phrasing and consistent with his instructional writing. So the passage as a whole is plausibly his composition even though its opening maxim is inherited. No source located.

results.earliest_print_source: Way of the Peaceful Warrior: A Book That Changes Lives, Dan Millman, 1980
results.notes: The signature line of Millman's Way of the Peaceful Warrior, spoken by the Socrates character, and the book's central teaching. It later titled his 1992 follow-up No Ordinary Moments and served as the tagline for the 2006 film adaptation, Peaceful Warrior. Attribution and source work are both solid; I have not verified a page number.

results.earliest_print_source: Way of the Peaceful Warrior, Dan Millman, 1980 (widely cited to this book; page/edition unverified)
results.notes: I recall this line as spoken by the 'Socrates' character in Millman's Way of the Peaceful Warrior (1980), usually quoted as 'Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't really live at all.' The attribution to Millman is consistent everywhere I have seen it and the voice matches the book. I cannot confirm the exact page or edition from memory, so I am holding this below the primary-source band.

Circulates widely and consistently under Dan Millman's name, but I cannot place it in any specific book of his. The sentiment is close to his 'peaceful warrior' material, which makes the attribution plausible rather than evidenced. No primary source known to me.

Reads like Millman's prose and likely comes from Everyday Enlightenment: The Twelve Gateways to Personal Growth (1998), which contains a gateway on managing finances framed around sufficiency rather than wealth or poverty. I cannot confirm the passage, so I am not asserting that book as the source.

This passage is consistently attributed to Dave Ramsey and matches his voice and his standard theme that money behavior reveals character. It most likely comes from The Total Money Makeover or the Financial Peace material, but I cannot pin the book or page, so no print source is asserted. Attribution is strong; the citation is not.

Standardly attributed to broadcaster David Brinkley (usually as 'A successful man is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks others have thrown at him'), but I know of no speech, broadcast, or book of his where it originates. Variants of the 'foundation from thrown bricks' aphorism circulated in American inspirational writing before Brinkley's prominence, which makes him a plausible popularizer rather than a confirmed author. The text here has also been gender-neutralized from the common form.

results.earliest_print_source: The Philosophy of Despair, David Starr Jordan, 1902 (widely cited; exact page unverified)
results.notes: Genuine David Starr Jordan, the Stanford naturalist and first president of the university. The original reads 'The world turns aside to let any man pass who knows whither he is going' and is commonly cited to his 1902 essay The Philosophy of Despair. The corpus records the author as 'David S. Jordan'; the standard form of the name is David Starr Jordan. The quote text here has been gender-neutralized from the original.
results.suggested_reattribution: David Starr Jordan (name normalization, same person)

results.notes: Attributed to David J. Schwartz and generally traced to The Magic of Thinking Big (1959), whose chapter on goals argues exactly this. The attribution is consistent and the source book is very likely correct, but I cannot verify the wording or page from memory, so I am leaving the print citation blank rather than asserting it. Note the corpus records the author as 'David Schwartz'; the usual byline is David J. Schwartz.

Attributed to singer Debby Boone across quote compilations, with no primary source I can identify — no book, interview, or speech. The attribution is uniform but rests entirely on quote-site repetition, which is weak evidence.

A signature Dee Hock line, from the Visa founder's chaordic-organization material. It was widely circulated after the 1996 Fast Company profile of Hock and appears in the same vein as Birth of the Chaordic Age (1999). Attribution to Hock is strong and consistent; I cannot confirm which of the two is the earliest print appearance, so I am not asserting a citation.

Chopra's vocabulary — 'conscious choice-maker' and actions that are 'evolutionary' are his terms from the Law of Karma chapter of The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success (1994). Attribution to Chopra is solid; I cannot confirm this exact sentence, so it may be a condensation of the passage rather than a verbatim line.

Widely quoted as Chopra and consistent with his teaching on non-resistance, but I cannot place it in any of his books or talks. Short aphorisms like this one attach easily to famous teachers, so I am keeping this well below the promotion bar.

results.earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Least Effort chapter (locus from memory, page unverified)
results.notes: This is the acceptance component of the Law of Least Effort in The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, where Chopra defines acceptance as agreeing to accept this moment as it is because struggling against it is struggling against the whole universe. I am confident in the book and chapter; I cannot verify the exact wording or page.

results.earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Intention and Desire chapter (page unverified)
results.notes: A well-known passage from the Law of Intention and Desire chapter; 'attention energizes, and intention transforms' and 'intention organizes its own fulfillment' are Chopra's exact formulations from that book. Strong attribution; I have not confirmed the page, so I am not claiming primary-source verification.

results.earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Dharma chapter (page unverified)
results.notes: This is essentially the opening statement of the Law of Dharma chapter, where Chopra states that everyone has a purpose and a unique talent, and that blending that talent with service to others is the goal of goals. Attribution and book are secure in my knowledge; the ellipsis suggests light editing from the original sentence.

The language is unmistakably Chopra's Vedanta framing — unity consciousness, the unified field, 'the seer and the scenery are one' — and it is consistently credited to him. I cannot place which book it comes from (candidates include The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success and Ageless Body, Timeless Mind), so I am not asserting a source.

One of the most widely circulated Denis Waitley lines, attributed to him uniformly across compilations and consistent with his Seeds of Greatness material. No primary source known to me, so the attribution is strong by repetition rather than by citation.

I have no knowledge of Denise Trifiletti or of this passage. The length and register suggest it was excerpted from a contributed essay in a multi-author inspirational anthology rather than being a circulating quotation. I cannot confirm or dispute the attribution — the honest answer here is that I do not know.

Attributed to Dhyani Ywahoo, the Cherokee teacher and author of Voices of Our Ancestors (1987), which would be the natural source. I recall the attribution but cannot confirm the passage in that book or any other, so the citation stays open.

Diana Hunt co-authored The Tao of Time (1990) with Pam Hait, and this line's theme of busyness as the measure of time fits that book, which is presumably why it is credited to her. I cannot verify the passage, and where a book has two authors an unattributed excerpt is doubly uncertain.

results.earliest_print_source: Third Olynthiac, Demosthenes, 349 BCE
results.notes: This is Demosthenes, not Diane Arbus. The line is a standard English rendering from the Third Olynthiac: 'Nothing is easier than self-deceit. For what each man wishes, that he also believes to be true.' It has nothing to do with photography and predates Arbus by well over two millennia.
