results.notes: Item five of the 'Seven Social Sins'. Same provenance as q_0641 — published by Gandhi, composed (on the best available account) by Frederick Lewis Donaldson for a Westminster Abbey sermon in March 1925. Fragment, not a standalone quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Young India, 22 October 1925 (Gandhi printed the list, crediting an unnamed correspondent)
results.notes: Item six of the 'Seven Social Sins'. Same provenance as q_0641. Fragment, not a standalone quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Young India, 22 October 1925 (Gandhi printed the list, crediting an unnamed correspondent)
results.notes: Item seven of the 'Seven Social Sins'. Same provenance as q_0641. Note the text here is pluralised — the canonical item is 'Politics without principle', singular — which suggests this set was transcribed from a secondary retelling rather than from the Young India text. Fragment, not a standalone quotation.

This item is NOT part of the 1925 'Seven Social Sins' list at all — the seven end at 'Politics without principle'. 'Rights without responsibilities' is a later addition; my understanding is that Arun Gandhi, M. K. Gandhi's grandson, has described appending an eighth item in this wording to the list his grandfather gave him. So attributing it to Mahatma Gandhi is wrong on both counts: he neither authored the original list nor included this line. I am moderately but not fully confident of the Arun Gandhi attribution, hence the low confidence and the empty citation field.
results.suggested_reattribution: Arun Gandhi (added as an eighth item to the list attributed to his grandfather)

results.notes: The vocabulary is distinctively Gary Zukav's — 'emotional currents', 'the quality of your light' are core terms of art in The Seat of the Soul (1989), and I believe that is where this passage comes from. Attribution to Zukav is not in doubt; I am withholding the book citation only because I cannot confirm the passage's placement well enough to enter it as a source. Held just below the promotion bar for that reason.

Circulates credited to Gary Zukav but I cannot place it in The Seat of the Soul or any other book of his, and the register is wrong for him — the pleading second-person address ('Please… tell me who you are and what you want') reads as dialogue from a novel, film, or television script rather than as Zukav's expository prose. The 'who are you / what do you want' pairing is also a widely circulated dramatic device, which raises the possibility of a transfer from a fictional source. Not enough basis to name an alternative author, so no reattribution offered.

Circulates almost exclusively on quotation aggregator sites credited to 'Geoffrey F. Abert', a name I cannot connect to any book, article, or biography in my training knowledge. No context, no date, no work. This pattern — a memorable aphorism bound to an otherwise undocumented name — usually means the attribution was copied from one quote list to the next without a source. I cannot confirm the person exists as an author, and I cannot place the line anywhere else.

Consistently and, I believe, correctly attributed to Shaw; the diction and the argumentative turn ('in the sense of phenomena we cannot explain') are characteristically his, and it appears in Shaw quotation collections rather than in the generic misattribution churn. My recollection places it in the long Preface to 'Back to Methuselah' (1921), where Shaw discusses miracles and creative evolution, but I am not confident enough in that placement to record it as a citation, so I have left the print source null. Shaw authorship: likely. Exact work: unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Man and Superman, George Bernard Shaw, 1903 (Epistle Dedicatory to Arthur Bingham Walkley)
results.notes: Genuine Shaw, from the Epistle Dedicatory prefacing 'Man and Superman' (1903). The surrounding passage runs: 'This is the true joy in life, the being used for a purpose recognized by yourself as a mighty one... I want to be thoroughly used up when I die, for the harder I work, the more I live. I rejoice in life for its own sake. Life is no brief candle to me. It is a sort of splendid torch which I have got hold of for the moment, and I want to make it burn as brightly as possible before handing it on to future generations.' Wording note for the corpus: the original reads 'which I have got hold of for the moment', not 'which I have got to hold up for the moment'. Recommend correcting the text to match the source.

results.earliest_print_source: Man and Superman, George Bernard Shaw, 1903 (Epistle Dedicatory to Arthur Bingham Walkley)
results.notes: Same passage as q_0653 — the two records are adjacent sentences from the Epistle Dedicatory to 'Man and Superman' (1903). Important wording note: Shaw wrote 'for the harder I work, the more I LIVE', not 'the more I love'. The corpus text carries a corrupted variant that inverts the sense of the line (Shaw's point is vitality, not affection). Attribution verified; text should be corrected. Consider also whether q_0653 and q_0654 should be merged into the single passage they came from.

Widely credited to Shaw and epigrammatic in his manner, but I cannot place it in any Shaw play, preface, essay, or in the 'Maxims for Revolutionists' appended to Man and Superman, which is where his freestanding aphorisms usually live. Absent a work I can name, and given how readily unsourced epigrams attach themselves to Shaw, I am treating the attribution as plausible but unsupported rather than strong.

results.earliest_print_source: Back to Methuselah, George Bernard Shaw, 1921 (Part I, Act I)
results.notes: Genuine Shaw. Spoken by the Serpent to Eve in Part I ('In the Beginning') of 'Back to Methuselah' (1921). Widely known in Robert F. Kennedy's paraphrase — 'Some men see things as they are and say why; I dream things that never were and say why not' — which RFK used in his 1968 campaign and which is sometimes mistaken for the original; Kennedy credited Shaw. The text as recorded here matches Shaw's wording. Note the corpus text carries stray wrapping double quotes around the whole line that should probably be stripped.

The pre-flag is correct: there is no Shaw source for this, and it appears in the misattributed section of Shaw quotation references. The saying circulated in the early twentieth century in the form 'Men do not quit playing because they grow old; they grow old because they quit playing', where it was credited to Oliver Wendell Holmes (Sr.). The Shaw credit, and the separate Satchel Paige credit, both appear to be later reassignments to more famous names. I am confident the Shaw attribution is wrong; I am only moderately confident in the Holmes origin, and the earliest instances may well be anonymous.
results.suggested_reattribution: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (earliest common attribution; possibly anonymous in origin) — not Shaw

results.earliest_print_source: Muriel Strode, 'Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers', The Open Court, 1903
results.notes: Not Shaw. This line is one of the most heavily reassigned aphorisms in circulation — most often pinned on Emerson, sometimes on Shaw, occasionally on Thoreau, with no support for any of them. The earliest known form is by the American poet Muriel Strode, published in 1903: 'I will not follow where the path may lead, but I will go where there is no path, and I will leave a trail.' The familiar imperative phrasing here is a later condensation of Strode's first-person original. I am confident the Shaw credit is wrong and reasonably confident in the Strode origin, though I am recalling the 1903 Open Court citation from memory and it should be spot-checked before the corpus leans on it.

results.earliest_print_source: Annajanska, the Bolshevik Empress, George Bernard Shaw, 1918
results.notes: Genuine Shaw, from the one-act 'Annajanska, the Bolshevik Empress' (first performed 1918, published shortly after). Correct wording is 'All great truths begin as blasphemies' — the corpus text reads 'Al great truths', a clear typo that should be fixed. Attribution itself is solid and consistently sourced to this play.

The joke is real but the ownership is contested and older than Burns. The underlying gag — 'The secret of success is sincerity; once you can fake that you've got it made' — is credited in several quotation dictionaries to Jean Giraudoux, and has also been pinned on Sam Goldwyn, Daniel Schorr, and others. The acting-specific variant given here is very commonly hung on George Burns, but I know of no interview, book, or routine of his where it can be located. Burns may well have used it; he did not originate it. I cannot establish who did, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing between the claimants.

Reads as authentic George Eliot — the cadence, the moral vocabulary ('trust and reverence'), and the aphoristic narrator's voice all fit her novels, and it is consistently attributed to her with no rival claimant. My impression is that it comes from 'Romola' (1863), but I cannot fix the chapter or confirm the novel, so I have left the print source null rather than record a guess as a citation. Eliot authorship: likely. Work: unconfirmed.

Almost certainly genuine George Eliot; this is narrative commentary of exactly the kind her novels carry, and it is quoted with consistent attribution. My recollection places it in 'Adam Bede' (1859), in the aftermath of Hetty's catastrophe, but I am not confident enough in the chapter or even the novel to record it as a citation. Attribution to Eliot: strong. Specific source: unconfirmed, and should be located in the text before this is promoted.

Plausibly George Lucas and consistent with how he has talked about the making of the first Star Wars film, but the wording is conversational, which suggests an interview or a documentary rather than a written source. I cannot identify which interview, publication, or year, and unsourced interview quotes drift easily. Attribution is credible but unsupported by anything I can name.

Circulates in design literature and Herman Miller-adjacent material credited to George Nelson, and the sentiment matches his writing on process (notably 'How to See' and his collected essays). I regard the attribution as credible but I cannot locate the sentence in a specific essay, lecture, or book, and design-world aphorisms are frequently paraphrased into tighter form than the original. Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be cited.

results.earliest_print_source: The Richest Man in Babylon, George S. Clason, 1926
results.notes: The author name in the record is misspelled: it should be George S. CLASON, not 'Claso'. The line belongs to Clason's parable collection 'The Richest Man in Babylon' (assembled from pamphlets of the early 1920s, published as a book in 1926), whose deliberately archaic maxim style — 'a lean purse' — this matches exactly. I am recalling the placement rather than reading it, so the citation is offered with that caveat, but the pairing of phrasing and author is distinctive enough that I do not consider it a guess. Fix the surname before promoting.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Carver, with no competing claimant, and it appears in Carver-specific material rather than only in general quote lists. I cannot connect it to a particular letter, address, or Tuskegee publication, and Carver's popular quotations are often transmitted through biographies and memorials rather than primary documents. Credible attribution, unconfirmed source; deliberately held below the promotion bar.

One of the most durable Carver sayings, transmitted through his advice to Tuskegee students and reproduced in Carver biographies and at the Carver National Monument. Attribution is consistent and I have no reason to doubt it; what I lack is a datable primary document — a letter, a speech text, or a published address — that fixes it. Somewhat better evidenced than q_0666 but still short of a citation.

Genuine O'Keeffe in substance — this is a documented position of hers from the 1920s, when she was arguing that women artists had territory of their own to work, and the phrasing appears in O'Keeffe letters-and-writings collections rather than only in quote aggregators. I believe it originates in her correspondence (the Anita Pollitzer letters are the likeliest home) or in a statement to the press around her early exhibitions, but I cannot pin the letter or the date, so no citation is recorded.

Consistent with Gerald Jampolsky's attitudinal-healing writing and consistently credited to him; the likeliest home is 'Love Is Letting Go of Fear' (1979) or 'Teach Only Love' (1983). I cannot confirm which, and self-help aphorisms are frequently condensed by readers into tighter form than the published sentence, so the wording may be a paraphrase even if the thought is his. Attribution credible, source unconfirmed.

The repetition-and-qualification rhythm ('doing nothing, really doing nothing') is unmistakably Stein, and the attribution is consistent. My recollection places it in 'The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas' (1933), where Stein-as-Toklas comments on Stein's working habits, but I cannot confirm the page or rule out 'Everybody's Autobiography'. Stein authorship: strong. Work: unconfirmed, so no citation recorded.

results.earliest_print_source: Everybody's Autobiography, Gertrude Stein, 1937
results.notes: The thought is verified Stein — from 'Everybody's Autobiography' (1937), where she describes returning to Oakland to find her childhood home gone: '...there is no there there.' The wording in this record is NOT hers. 'When you get there, there isn't any there there' is a loose popular restatement; the canonical line is 'there is no there there'. Attribution to Stein is solid, so I have not marked it misattributed, but the text should be corrected to the published wording (and ideally given its Oakland context) before promotion — as it stands the corpus would be quoting the paraphrase, not the source. The 'spirit' category also misreads the line, which is about a vanished place, not transcendence.

'Glenda Cloud' is a name that exists, so far as I can tell, only as an attribution line on quotation sites — I can connect it to no book, article, speech, or biography. The aphorism itself is a compact motivational formula of the kind that circulates anonymously and then acquires a plausible-sounding name. Honest answer: origin unknown, and I have no basis for either confirming or reassigning it.

Glenn Clark (1882-1956) was a real author in the American devotional and prayer tradition — 'The Man Who Talks with the Flowers', 'How to Find Health through Prayer' — and the sentiment and register fit his work well, so the attribution is at least plausible rather than arbitrary. But I cannot locate the sentence in any of his books, and the 'travel light' framing is common enough in inspirational writing that convergence is possible. Plausible attribution, no source I can name.

Steinem is the standard credit and she has used the line in talks, so this is not a case of a name attached at random. But it is a variant of an older saying rather than an original coinage: forms such as 'The truth will set you free, but first it will make you miserable' were in circulation well before her, sometimes credited to James A. Garfield. Steinem's contribution is the sharpened profanity, and even that I cannot fix to a datable speech, essay, or interview. Best read as popularized-by rather than originated-by; holding well below the promotion bar.

This is a translation of the German 'Nichts ist mehr wert als dieser Tag', which I believe to be genuine Goethe, most likely from his gnomic verse or aphorism collections ('Sprichwortlich' or the 'Maximen und Reflexionen'). I cannot fix the collection or the year, so no citation is recorded. Worth flagging that Goethe is a heavy misattribution magnet in English — the famous 'Whatever you can do or dream you can, begin it' is a John Anster paraphrase of Faust filtered through W.H. Murray and is not Goethe's — but this short line does not fit that pattern and I have no evidence against it. Also note the author field should probably read 'Johann Wolfgang von Goethe'.

results.earliest_print_source: The Scottish Himalayan Expedition, W. H. Murray, 1951
results.notes: One of the best-documented Goethe misattributions. The prose passage ('Until one is committed... a whole stream of events issues from the decision') is W. H. Murray, from the opening of The Scottish Himalayan Expedition (1951). Murray closed the passage by quoting a couplet he credited to Goethe; that couplet ('Whatever you can do, or dream you can, begin it. Boldness has genius, power, and magic in it.') is in fact John Anster's very loose 1835 verse rendering of a passage in the 'Vorspiel auf dem Theater' of Faust, not a literal Goethe line. The Goethe Society of North America has publicly addressed this attribution. Nothing in the paragraph is Goethe's own prose.
results.suggested_reattribution: W. H. Murray (prose); closing couplet is John Anster's 1835 loose translation of Goethe's Faust

results.notes: A German original circulates ('Je alter ich werde, desto mehr vertraue ich auf das Gesetz, wonach die Rose und die Lilie bluhen'), and the sentiment and diction are consistent with late Goethe, which raises my prior that it is genuine rather than invented. But I cannot place it in a specific work, letter, or conversation from what I know, and Goethe is a heavily aggregated quote-collection author. Honest verdict: plausible but unplaced.

Consistently attributed to Golda Meir across quotation collections, and the sentiment fits her documented working style, but I cannot place it in her memoir My Life (1975), in a speech, or in a contemporaneous interview. No competing attribution known to me. Attribution is stable but unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Los Caprichos, plate 43 ('El sueno de la razon produce monstruos'), Francisco Goya, 1799 — author's explanatory commentary (Prado manuscript)
results.notes: This is Goya's own gloss on Capricho No. 43. The manuscript commentaries to Los Caprichos (the Prado set) explain plate 43 with essentially this text: imagination abandoned by reason produces impossible monsters; united with reason it is the mother of the arts and the source of their wonders. The line is Goya's, tied to a specific dated work. Slight variance across English translations ('fantasy'/'imagination', 'marvels'/'wonders') is translation drift, not attribution doubt. Confidence held just below 0.9 because the commentary survives in manuscript and its precise wording varies by edition.

Grace Lichtenstein is a real American journalist and author (New York Times reporter; wrote on women in sport and the American West), so the attribution is not to a fictitious person. But I cannot place this line in any of her books or articles. It reads like an anthology extract, possibly from an adventure- or women's-outdoors collection. Unplaced.

Greg Anderson is a real wellness author (The 22 Non-Negotiable Laws of Wellness, 1995; The Cancer Conqueror), and this line is routinely credited to him in quotation databases, but I cannot confirm which book it comes from or that it originates with him rather than with a compiler. Common-name risk as well: several authors named Greg Anderson exist. Unplaced.

I recognize this as a line from Shantaram (Gregory David Roberts, 2003) — it belongs to the Khaderbhai passages on good, evil, and the universe tending toward complexity and God. I am confident about the novel; I cannot cite chapter or page, and the circulating version may be lightly compressed from the original paragraph. Note it is dialogue spoken by a character, which is worth flagging if the corpus distinguishes author voice from character voice.

Groucho Marx is a first-rank misattribution magnet — a large share of quips credited to him were written by his screenwriters, said by other comedians, or attached to his name later. I cannot place this line in a film, a Groucho book (Groucho and Me, Memoirs of a Mangy Lover), or a documented broadcast. The construction is stylistically plausible for him, which is precisely the weakest kind of evidence. Treat as unverified.

The vocabulary is authentically Gurdjieffian — 'real love' as objective rather than subjective, and 'crystallize' as a technical term in the Fourth Way system — so this is unlikely to be a wholesale invention. Gurdjieff's talks reach us mostly through pupils' transcriptions (Views from the Real World, Ouspensky's In Search of the Miraculous), so wording is inherently secondhand. I cannot place this specific sentence in a particular talk or transcript.

Reported of Flaubert by Guy de Maupassant, who in his essay-preface to Pierre et Jean (1887-88) recounts Flaubert's instruction to him that talent is a long patience ('Le talent est une longue patience'). So the attribution rests on a strong, named, contemporaneous witness rather than on Flaubert's own pen. Also worth flagging a precursor: Buffon is credited with 'Le genie n'est qu'une plus grande aptitude a la patience,' and the two sayings are frequently conflated. Kept below the promotion bar because the line is a pupil's report of speech, not a Flaubert text.

Widely circulated over H. G. Wells's name in inspirational collections, but I cannot place it in his novels, essays, journalism, or the Experiment in Autobiography. The register is warmer and more devotional than Wells's characteristic prose, which mildly argues against it. No alternative author known to me. Unverified.

This is a genuine and much-repeated Tenzin Gyatso formulation — the 'necessities, not luxuries' framing of compassion recurs across his public teaching and writing. I have a moderate recollection that it appears in the vicinity of his 1989 Nobel Peace Prize lecture in Oslo and in later compassion-focused books, but I am not confident enough in the specific venue to record it as a citation, so earliest_print_source is left null rather than guessed. Attribution to the Dalai Lama itself is solid; the sourcing is not.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Divine Afflatus', H. L. Mencken, New York Evening Mail, 16 November 1917; collected in Prejudices: Second Series, 1920
results.notes: The idea is authentically Mencken's but the wording here is a later paraphrase. Mencken's actual sentence is: 'there is always a well-known solution to every human problem — neat, plausible, and wrong.' The circulating 'For every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple, and wrong' is a rewrite that swaps his adjectives and adds 'complex'. Author is right; text is not his. Recommend replacing the text with Mencken's original wording, at which point this becomes a clean verified entry.

results.earliest_print_source: The Gift: Poems by Hafiz the Great Sufi Master, Daniel Ladinsky, 1999
results.notes: This is Daniel Ladinsky's poem 'Pulling Out the Chair', not a translation of the 14th-century Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz. Ladinsky has stated that his 'Hafiz' books are not translations from Persian — he does not read Persian — and scholars of Persian literature (Omid Safi among others) have documented that these poems have no counterparts in the Divan. The overwhelming majority of English 'Hafiz' quotations in circulation are Ladinsky originals, this one included.

Same problem as the preceding Hafiz entry. The diction — 'knee-deep in ecstasy', 'all your talents to love' — is characteristic of Daniel Ladinsky's English compositions (The Gift, 1999; I Heard God Laughing, 1996), which are presented as Hafiz but have no basis in the Persian Divan. I cannot name the specific Ladinsky poem, so the reattribution is a strong inference from provenance patterns and style rather than a placed citation; earliest_print_source left null accordingly. What I am confident of is the negative: this is not a rendering of Hafez of Shiraz.
results.suggested_reattribution: Daniel Ladinsky (probable — his 'Hafiz' poems are original English works, not translations)

results.notes: Consistently and, I believe, correctly credited to the painter and teacher Hans Hofmann; my recollection associates it with his essay collection Search for the Real and Other Essays (1948), which is where his aphoristic statements on pictorial means are gathered. I am not confident enough of that placement to record it as a citation. The line is a staple of design literature, so anthology-drift is possible in the wording.

The author name in the record is a well-known corruption. There is no 'Harold Thurman Whitman'; the name is a mangling of Howard Thurman (1899-1981), the African-American theologian and mentor to civil rights leaders. The attribution chain runs through Gil Bailie, who in Violence Unveiled (1995) reports this as spoken advice Thurman gave him. It has not been located in Thurman's own published writings, so even under the corrected name it is a secondhand report of speech rather than a sourced text. At minimum the author field should be fixed to Howard Thurman; the quote should not be promoted as verified.

Long-standing and stable attribution to Harriet Beecher Stowe, appearing in quotation collections well back into the 20th century, which argues against recent invention. I cannot place it in Uncle Tom's Cabin, Oldtown Folks, her letters, or her domestic essays, and I do not know whether it is authorial prose or a line given to a character. Plausible but unsourced.

A modern motivational composition attached to Harriet Tubman; it appears in the misattributed section of her Wikiquote page. Tubman did not read or write, and her documented words reach us through Sarah Bradford's Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869) and a small number of interviews and dictated letters — none of which contain anything like this. The register ('reach for the stars to change the world') is late-20th-century inspirational English, not 19th-century speech. No true author known to me, hence apocryphal rather than a reattribution. Recommend rejection rather than correction.

Credited to Harry Emerson Fosdick, the liberal Protestant preacher of Riverside Church, and the theme — faith enlarged rather than threatened by mystery — is squarely his. Fosdick preached and published prolifically (The Meaning of Faith, On Being a Real Person, decades of sermons), so a genuine origin is quite possible, but I cannot place the sentence in a specific sermon or book. Fosdick is not a misattribution magnet, which slightly raises confidence, but the source is unfound.

Widely credited to Helen Keller and consistent with her published voice; she wrote a great deal (The Story of My Life, Optimism, Out of the Dark, My Religion, extensive correspondence), so many Keller quotations are genuine. I cannot place this particular sentence in a specific work. Plausible, unsourced.

I am reasonably confident this is genuine Keller and associate it with her essay Optimism (1903), though not confidently enough to record that as a citation. Important textual note: the standard wording is 'sailed to an uncharted land, or opened a new doorway for the human spirit.' The record here reads 'an enchanted land' and 'to the human spirit' — 'enchanted' is a common corruption of 'uncharted' and should be corrected before the quote is used. Confidence held at 0.6 because the text as stored is drifted even though the attribution looks sound.

A very widely circulated Keller line with a stable attribution going back decades, and thematically continuous with her writing on optimism and adversity. My recollection associates it loosely with her letters or her essay writing rather than with a book I can name, so I will not record a source. Attribution more likely genuine than not, but unverified.

Consistently attributed to Helen Keller; the phrasing ('fidelity to a worthy purpose') has an early-20th-century cast that fits her period and prose, unlike the modern-sounding lines often invented for her. I cannot place it in a specific essay, book, or letter. Plausible, unsourced.

This one deserves skepticism despite its fame. It circulates in several mutually inconsistent forms — 'The greatest tragedy in life is people who have sight but no vision', 'The only thing worse than being blind is having sight but no vision', 'Worse than being blind is to see and have no vision' — and variant proliferation with no fixed wording is a classic signature of apocrypha. I cannot place any version in Keller's substantial published corpus, and the epigram has the shape of a line composed for her because she was blind. Not called outright apocryphal only because her writings are extensive enough that I cannot exclude an origin I simply do not recall. Do not promote.

results.earliest_print_source: We Bereaved, Helen Keller, 1929
results.notes: I recall this being sourced on Wikiquote's Helen Keller page to her 1929 book We Bereaved, with the original reading '...the one which has been opened for us.' The bare proverb 'when one door closes, another opens' is older and is often credited to Alexander Graham Bell (Keller's friend); Keller's contribution is the second clause about staring at the closed door. Confident in Keller as author, moderately confident in the 1929 book as the print locus.

results.earliest_print_source: The Open Door, Helen Keller, 1957
results.notes: Genuinely Keller. The full passage runs 'Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure or nothing.' Standard citation is The Open Door (1957); some sources instead point to Let Us Have Faith (1940). Author attribution is solid; I am less certain which of the two volumes is the first printing, so I am holding below verified.

results.earliest_print_source: Creative Evolution (L'Evolution creatrice), Henri Bergson, 1907
results.notes: From Creative Evolution, ch. 1. The original opens with a qualifier the corpus text drops: 'For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.' Primary source confirmed; only the truncation is at issue, and it does not alter the sense.

results.earliest_print_source: Journal Intime (Amiel's Journal), Henri-Frederic Amiel, trans. Mrs. Humphry Ward, 1885
results.notes: Amiel's aphorisms nearly all come from the Journal Intime, published posthumously and Englished by Mrs. Humphry Ward in 1885; this line reads as authentic Ward-translation Amiel and is consistently attributed to him. I cannot recall the dated journal entry it belongs to, so I am not claiming a page-level verification.

Consistently attributed to Amiel and stylistically of a piece with the Journal Intime, which is the source of essentially all circulating Amiel quotations. I cannot place the specific entry or confirm the translation used, so no print source is claimed.

Widely circulated under Matisse's name in quotation anthologies. I cannot place it in Notes of a Painter (1908), Jazz (1947), or the Flam collection of Matisse's writings, and the phrasing reads more like an English aphorism than a translation from Matisse's French. Plausible but unconfirmed; the sentiment about the resistance of the medium is genuinely Matissean, which is not evidence of authorship.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden, Henry David Thoreau, 1854 (chapter 'Higher Laws')
results.notes: Genuine Thoreau, from the 'Higher Laws' chapter of Walden. The original reads 'a miracle which is taking place every instant' — the corpus text substitutes 'every second,' a common circulating variant. Recommend restoring 'instant' if the corpus prefers original wording.

I do not believe this paragraph appears anywhere in Thoreau. It reads as a later self-help expansion of a genuine passage in Walden's 'Conclusion': 'It is remarkable how easily and insensibly we fall into a particular route, and make a beaten track for ourselves... The surface of the earth is soft and impressible by the feet of men; and so with the paths which the mind travels.' The 'single footstep / single thought / think over and over the kind of thoughts we wish to dominate our lives' construction is characteristic of twentieth-century New Thought prose, not Thoreau's. I cannot name the actual writer who composed the expansion, so no reattribution is offered.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden, Henry David Thoreau, 1854 (chapter 'Conclusion')
results.notes: Verbatim Thoreau from the 'Conclusion' of Walden. Short, exact, and correctly attributed.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden, Henry David Thoreau, 1854 (chapter 'Conclusion')
results.notes: Both halves are genuine Walden, from 'Conclusion,' but the corpus text is the popular second-person paraphrase. Thoreau wrote in the third person: 'I learned this, at least, by my experiment: that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.' The passage also compresses the original ('he will put some things behind, will pass an invisible boundary'; 'he will live with the license of a higher order of beings') and the castles line ends 'Now put the foundations under them,' plural. Source certain; wording modernized.

results.earliest_print_source: The Greatest Thing in the World, Henry Drummond, c. 1887
results.notes: Consistently attributed to Drummond's famous address on 1 Corinthians 13, delivered in the mid-1880s and printed as The Greatest Thing in the World. The sentiment and cadence match that text closely. I am not certain of the exact publication year (the address circulated from 1884 and the book appeared later in the decade) and cannot confirm the page, so the year above is approximate rather than a verified citation.

No evidence Ford ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator examined it and found no attribution to Ford during his lifetime; the earliest linkages surface in business and marketing literature around the turn of the twenty-first century, decades after his 1947 death. It does not appear in My Life and Work (1922). Wikiquote carries it as disputed/unsourced. No true originator is identifiable, so I am marking it apocryphal rather than reattributing.

The core sentence — 'the only real security a man can have in this world is a reserve of knowledge, experience and ability' — is very consistently attributed to Ford and is compatible with his views on money as a tool in My Life and Work (1922) and his Dearborn Independent pieces. I cannot place the full paragraph in a specific Ford text, and the surrounding sentences may be an anthologist's assembly. Plausibly genuine, unconfirmed; keeping it below the promotion bar.

Ford is a misattribution magnet, and this is one of the borderline cases. The saying does not appear in Ford's own writings as far as I know; the earliest attribution to him that I recall from Quote Investigator's treatment is a Reader's Digest filler item in 1947, the year Ford died — a secondhand ascription, not a source. Circulating wording is usually 'Whether you think you can, or you think you can't, you're right,' without the corpus text's 'probably.' Attribution is traditional rather than documented.

Known only as a reported remark, not as anything James published. The tradition traces to a recollection by James's nephew (Billy James), passed into the biographical literature and the collections of Jamesian anecdote; there is no primary text. It is also frequently confused with William James. Plausibly a real spoken remark, but unverifiable from what I know. Note that q_0716 is a near-duplicate of this entry, differing only by an 'And' — the corpus should keep one.

Duplicate of q_0715 with 'And the third' shortened to 'The third'; same verdict. Secondhand anecdote attributed to Henry James via his nephew's recollection, with no primary text and recurring confusion with William James. Recommend deduplicating against q_0715 and preferring whichever wording the source anthology used.

The form I have encountered is 'The full and joyful acceptance of the worst in oneself may be the only sure way of transforming it' — the corpus text has softened 'the worst in oneself' to 'the self' and hardened 'may be' to 'is,' which changes the meaning. Attributed to Henry Miller in quotation collections; I cannot place it in The Wisdom of the Heart, Big Sur and the Oranges of Hieronymus Bosch, or any other Miller volume. Uncertain both as to authorship and as to wording.

results.earliest_print_source: The Colossus of Maroussi, Henry Miller, 1941
results.notes: I am fairly confident this passage is from the closing pages of The Colossus of Maroussi, which contains the 'every moment is a golden one for him who has the vision to recognize it as such' line. The corpus text drops the 'it' in that final clause. Authorship confident; page-level citation not recalled, so short of verified.

Attributed to Miller across quotation sites, but I cannot locate it in any of his books and have no early citation for it. Possibly from an essay or interview, possibly an anthologist's condensation. Honest answer: I don't know where this comes from.

results.earliest_print_source: 'For Katrina's Sun-Dial,' Henry van Dyke, in Music and Other Poems, 1904
results.notes: Genuine van Dyke. Written as a sundial inscription for Katrina Trask at Yaddo and printed in his 1904 collection; the verse is set as short lines, which the corpus has run together as prose. Van Dyke wrote a second, shorter sundial verse ('Hours fly, flowers die...') that is sometimes conflated with this one.

Long and consistently attributed to van Dyke, and consonant with his essays, but I recall it sitting in the unsourced section of quotation references rather than being tied to a specific book or sermon. The usual wording includes 'no birds sang there except those that sang best,' which the corpus drops. Likely genuine, undocumented.

Attributed to van Dyke in anthologies; the homiletic register fits a Presbyterian preacher-essayist, and the line may come from a sermon or address. I cannot name the text, and I have no early citation. Unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Secret of the Sea,' Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, in The Seaside and the Fireside, 1850
results.notes: Genuine Longfellow, from the poem 'The Secret of the Sea.' The stanza is spoken in dialogue and the original is archaic: 'Wouldst thou' — so the helmsman answered — 'learn the secret of the sea? / Only those who brave its dangers / Comprehend its mystery!' The corpus text modernizes the opening and drops the helmsman frame. Poem attribution is certain; I am slightly less sure of the collecting volume, though The Seaside and the Fireside (1850) is my recollection.

Beecher's circulating aphorisms mostly derive from Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit (1887) and Life Thoughts (1858), compilations drawn from his preaching, and this line plausibly belongs to one of them. I cannot confirm which, or that it is Beecher's at all rather than a compiler's condensation of a longer passage. Unverified.

Very consistently attributed to Beecher and characteristic of his pulpit style; most likely from one of the Plymouth Pulpit compilations (Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit, 1887, or Life Thoughts, 1858). I cannot confirm the volume or page from memory, so no print source is claimed. Probably genuine but held below the promotion bar.

A standard Henny Youngman one-liner, consistently attributed to him across joke anthologies and obituary-era retrospectives; no competing attribution that I know of. I cannot place its first print appearance or a specific routine. Note the author field is misspelled: the comedian is Henny Youngman (1906-1998), not 'Henry'.

I know of no Heraclitus fragment resembling this. The surviving fragments (Diels-Kranz) concern logos, flux, fire, opposites, and the soul's depth - not 'personality', which is a post-classical and largely modern psychological concept. The vocabulary and the transcend/descend construction read as 20th-century spiritual writing. I cannot identify the real author, so I am not offering a reattribution.

Ubiquitously attributed to Herm Albright, usually with the dates 1876-1944 and sometimes with a credit to The Saturday Evening Post or Reader's Digest. I am not aware of anyone having located the line in a text Albright actually wrote, and Albright himself is an obscure figure (a German-American engraver) whose name appears in circulation almost solely as the tag on this one quote - a pattern typical of quote-anthology attributions that were never sourced. Plausible but unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Siddhartha, Hermann Hesse, 1922 (English: Hilda Rosner trans., New Directions, 1951)
results.notes: Genuine Hesse. This is from Siddhartha, in the closing conversation where Siddhartha speaks to Govinda by the river; the Rosner translation runs close to 'the world is not imperfect or slowly evolving along a long path to perfection... it is perfect at every moment; every sin already carries grace within it.' Exact wording varies by translation. Author field should read 'Hermann Hesse' (two n's).

results.earliest_print_source: Demian, Hermann Hesse, 1919
results.notes: Abraxas is the central symbol of Demian, and this is Pistorius speaking to Sinclair about the dreams one must not betray - 'you aren't allowed to be afraid of anything, you can't consider prohibited anything the soul desires.' I am confident of the work; the exact wording depends on translation, and the quote as stored is elided (leading ellipsis) and carries a stray closing quotation mark at the end that should be cleaned up.

Reads as authentic Hesse and is consistently attributed to him with no competing author. My recollection places it in the Narcissus and Goldmund / aphorism-collection territory (the English Reflections, ed. Volker Michels, gathers many such lines), but I cannot confirm the work, so I am not naming one. Attribution to Hesse is solid; the source is not.

I cannot place this in any Hesse work I know. The theological framing (self-affirmation as a precondition for affirming God) is compatible with Hesse's post-Demian thought but is also standard 20th-century Protestant-existentialist phrasing, so the resemblance is weak evidence. Short aphorisms of this shape circulate under Hesse's name from the Reflections compilation without individual sourcing. Honest answer: I do not know.

I cannot place this line in Hesse. The hedonist-to-mystic idea is thematically at home in Steppenwolf and Narcissus and Goldmund, but thematic fit is not evidence of authorship, and the epigrammatic English phrasing does not match any passage I can recall. Possible it derives from a compiler's condensation of a longer Hesse passage rather than a sentence he wrote. Unverified.

A long translated passage rather than an aphorism, which itself argues for authenticity - fabricated quotes are rarely this extended or this specific ('the blessed hermits... in their oasis among the deer'; 'in the pictures of a good painter, every tree and every mountain prays'). The voice and imagery are strongly Hesse. I believe it is genuine but I cannot identify which work it comes from, so I am leaving the source null rather than guessing between Narcissus and Goldmund, Wandering, and the essays.

The language is anachronistic for a 12th-century abbess. 'Creation... its endangerment' frames an ecological crisis that has no 12th-century counterpart, and 'rise vigorously toward justice' reads as modern social-justice idiom. Lines of this kind entered circulation through the Matthew Fox creation-spirituality treatments of Hildegard in the 1980s, which are loose renderings and adaptations rather than translations. I am fairly confident this is not a faithful Hildegard text, but I cannot pin the specific modern author or book, so I am not naming Fox as the source.

Folk-proverbial with no traceable source. Near-identical formulations appear across several traditions - a hadith qudsi ('if he draws near to Me a hand's span, I draw near to him an arm's length; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running'), a Talmudic version, and Sufi and Sikh retellings - which is the signature of a migrating saying rather than a fixed Hindu text. I know of no Sanskrit scriptural locus for the 'one step / seven steps' form.

I cannot trace this to any Hindu source. It resembles a widely retold parable in which the gods hide divinity inside the human being as the last place anyone would look - a story usually presented as 'Hindu legend' in Western popular writing but with no scriptural citation I know of. The epigram itself reads as a modern English formulation. Also note the typo in the stored text: 'chose' should be 'choose'.

A well-documented misattribution. The line does not appear in the Hippocratic Corpus; the standard reference on this is Diana Cardenas's 2013 paper in e-SPEN Journal, 'Let not thy food be confused with thy medicine: The Hippocratic misquotation', which searched the corpus and found no such statement, and which traces the saying's spread to 20th-century nutrition and natural-health writing. The Hippocratic texts do discuss diet as part of regimen, but that is a general theme, not this sentence. Treat any 'Hippocrates' tag on this as false; the true originator is not identifiable.

Attribution to Hodding Carter Jr. (1907-1972) is near-universal, but as far as I know nobody has located the sentence in anything Carter wrote or in a dated speech. Quote Investigator's work on 'roots and wings' found earlier and anonymous variants circulating before the Carter tag became standard, which suggests he popularized rather than coined it. The saying is also sometimes given as a 'Chinese proverb' or attributed to Goethe, both without support. Plausible but unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Horace, Epistles I.2, line 40 (c. 20 BCE): 'Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet'
results.notes: The Horatian line is genuine and is the usual ancestor cited for this English proverb, but it literally says 'he who has begun has half the deed done' - the 'well begun' element is the English proverb's addition. The same idea is older and Greek-proverbial (Hesiod's 'the beginning is half of the whole'; Aristotle quotes the proverb in the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics), so 'Well begun is half done' is better described as a proverb with a Horatian pedigree than as a Horace quotation. Attribution defensible, exact wording not his.

Consistently attributed to Hubert Selby Jr. with no competing author, and the cadence and preoccupations match him closely. My recollection is that it comes from a late-career interview or from the documentary material about him rather than from a novel, but I cannot pin a specific interview, publication, or date, so I am leaving the source null.

Consistently attributed to Selby and stylistically unmistakable - the vernacular register ('it's no big deal', 'worth the price of admission') alongside the life/death framing is his. Its length and specificity argue against fabrication. I recall it as coming from Selby's own prose or an interview about the work, but I cannot identify the piece, so no source is claimed.

Reads as authentic Huston Smith - 'relativized against this one absolute' is his comparative-religion register, and the primacy of astonishment over other marks of realization is a recurring Smith theme. I have a weak recollection of the phrasing but cannot place the book (Why Religion Matters, The Way Things Are, and Cleansing the Doors of Perception are all plausible and I will not guess among them). Attribution likely correct, source unverified.

A genuine IDEO maxim, closely associated with David Kelley and with the firm's design-thinking teaching materials; it circulates widely in innovation literature with the attribution to IDEO-as-organization held stable. I believe it appears in the Kelley brothers' published work on IDEO's method but I cannot confirm which book or page, so I am not citing one. Attributing to an organization rather than a person is itself appropriate here.

Attributed on quote aggregators to Ifeanyi Enoch Onuoha, a contemporary Nigerian author and speaker, but I know of no book, talk, or dated publication where it appears - aggregator-only attributions of this kind are weak evidence. The line is also a close derivative of the widely circulated Andrew Carnegie teamwork quotation ('the fuel that allows common people to attain uncommon results'), which is itself of doubtful Carnegie provenance. Possible restatement rather than original coinage.

A signature Imogen Cunningham line, given in interviews in her last years and repeated in profiles and documentary material about her; the attribution is stable and I am not aware of it being claimed for any other photographer. I cannot cite the specific interview or its date, so the source stays null, but the attribution itself is strong.

Untraceable and multiply claimed. The same saying circulates as an 'Indian proverb', a 'Native American proverb' (often tagged to a 'White Elk', a figure of doubtful historicity), a 'Cherokee saying', and in Persian and Islamic devotional forms. That spread across unrelated traditions is characteristic of a modern inspirational composition retrofitted with an exotic attribution. I know of no Sanskrit or other original text for it.

Consistently attributed to Indira Gandhi and internally coherent - her grandfather was Motilal Nehru, so the framing device fits her biography rather than being generic. It appears in political-quotation collections with the attribution stable. Note this is Indira Gandhi, not Mohandas Gandhi, so the usual Gandhi misattribution magnet does not apply here. I cannot cite the speech or interview of origin.

The attribution to an inscription at St Paul's Monastery on Mount Athos comes largely from Eckhart Tolle, who cites it that way in The Power of Now (1997). I am not aware of any independent documentation that the inscription exists or of a transcription by anyone who visited. The underlying formula is old and widespread - the Sufi and hadith-derived 'die before you die', and the Christian ascetic tradition of dying to self - so the sentiment is genuinely ancient even if this English epigram and its Athos provenance are not confirmable. Source claim unverified.

I cannot trace this to any proverb collection I know. Generic 'Irish proverb' tags are among the least reliable in quotation corpora - they are frequently applied to modern greeting-card sentiments and to translations of sayings from other traditions. The give-with-one-hand / gather-with-two structure is a common proverbial shape without a fixed home. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know.

Circulates widely in proverb collections and greeting-card compilations as an Irish saying, but I cannot place it in any Irish-language source, folklore collection, or dated print appearance. 'Irish Proverb' is a common catch-all label attached to humorous one-liners of uncertain origin. Honest answer: origin unknown; the folk-attribution is plausible but unevidenced.

Consistently and widely attributed to fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi, and the sentiment and phrasing match his public persona and interview style (his remarks around the 1995 documentary 'Unzipped' and later press). I cannot place the specific interview or publication, so no print source is given. Note the input text reads 'makes you feels great' — an apparent transcription error for 'makes you feel great'.

Appears in English-language proverb dictionaries under the Italian heading, likely rendering something on the order of 'Chi troppo fa, nulla fa' / 'Chi troppo vuole nulla stringe'. I cannot confirm a specific Italian original or an earliest print appearance. Generic proverb attribution, no traceable source.

I recall this as genuine Borges, from the story 'Deutsches Requiem' (collected in 'El Aleph', 1949; English in 'Labyrinths'), Spanish along the lines of 'Morir por una religión es más simple que vivirla con plenitud.' The attribution to Borges is strong and consistent; because I am recalling rather than verifying the exact volume and translation, I have left earliest_print_source null rather than assert a citation I cannot check.

I cannot place this in Kornfield's published work. The crucible/purification metaphor is common across contemporary spiritual writing and is not distinctively his idiom (his register tends toward the plainer and more psychological). No evidence of a specific book, talk, or dated source. Attribution unsupported by anything I actually know.

Strongly consistent with Jack Kornfield's voice and central themes — the ordinary present over exotic states, the 'wise and kindly heart', bowing to both beauty and suffering — and reads like a closing passage from 'A Path with Heart' (1993) or 'After the Ecstasy, the Laundry' (2000). I cannot confirm which book or page, so no citation is given. Author plausible and likely; source unlocated.

Idiomatically consistent with Kornfield (the theme of one's particular life as the vehicle of awakening runs through 'A Path with Heart'), but I cannot locate the passage. The 'Buddhism, Theravada' context tag matches his lineage and adds nothing independent. Author plausible; unverified.

Reads like transcribed spoken teaching — an interview or dharma talk rather than a book — which is a common source for quotes circulating under Kornfield's name and also a common source of loose paraphrase. The 'original goodness' framing is genuinely his, but I cannot tie this wording to a specific talk or publication.

Consistently attributed to the American talk-show host Jack Paar (1918-2004), whose self-deprecating style this matches; it is often associated with his memoir 'I Kid You Not' (1960), though I cannot confirm that placement. Note the author field misspells his surname as 'Parr' — it should be Paar. Attribution to Paar is solid; the print source is not.

Genuine Jack Welch, and I recall the fuller original as 'The world of the Nineties and beyond will not belong to managers or those who can make the numbers dance...' from his letter to shareholders in a General Electric annual report of the early 1990s (1991 is the year I associate with it). The quoted text here has clipped 'of the Nineties' out of the opening phrase, leaving the ungrammatical 'The world beyond'. Attribution strong; exact document and year recalled but not verified, so no citation asserted.

The attribution is doubtful. Jackie Gleason did have a serious documented interest in parapsychology and the occult and assembled a large library on it, which is probably why the name attracts material like this, but the diction here ('firsthand creations, rather than residues of waking life', 'the infinite Godhead that creates the cosmos') reads as academic dream-studies or transpersonal-psychology prose, not a comedian's remark. I suspect it originates in a book on dreaming and was later mislabeled, but I cannot identify the real author, so I am not proposing one.

The subject and framing match Jacob Needleman's 'Money and the Meaning of Life' (1991) closely enough that I believe it is his — the book is built on exactly this question of whether money imprisons or can be turned toward awakening. I cannot confirm the wording or locate the page, so the citation is left null rather than asserted from a topical match.

Compatible with Needleman's religious-philosophical writing ('Lost Christianity', 1980; 'The American Soul', 2002) and with the Gurdjieffian vocabulary of 'conscious life' and 'understanding heart' that runs through his work, but I cannot place the sentence in any specific book. Author plausible; source unlocated.

Jalaja Bonheim is a real author on embodied spirituality whose books include 'Aphrodite's Daughters' (1997) and 'The Hunger for Ecstasy' (2001); this line's subject matter points to the latter. The attribution is plausible and I know of no competing claimant, but I cannot confirm the passage, so this stays unverified.

This is a floating saying with many earlier variants ('Let no one who says it cannot be done interrupt the one doing it'; 'The person who says it cannot be done should not interrupt the person doing it'), circulating from the early twentieth century and credited over the years to a Chinese proverb, Confucius, George Bernard Shaw, and Elbert Hubbard — a pattern that indicates no settled origin. I have no evidence that any James Baldwin, novelist or otherwise, originated it, and the 'James A. Baldwin' form suggests a name that accreted rather than a documented author. Because I cannot identify the true origin, I am not proposing a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: As a Man Thinketh, James Allen, 1903
results.notes: Authentic James Allen, from the chapter 'Visions and Ideals' in 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903). The passage continues 'Cherish your visions; cherish your ideals...' The wording quoted here matches the standard text.

results.earliest_print_source: As a Man Thinketh, James Allen, 1903
results.notes: Authentic James Allen, from the opening chapter of 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903) on thought and character. The original uses the British spelling 'armoury'; the quoted text has Americanized it to 'armory', which is a spelling variant rather than a change of substance.

This is a splice of two different authors presented as one quotation. The first sentence, 'Our life is what our thoughts make it', is Marcus Aurelius, from the 'Meditations'. The second sentence is genuine James Allen, from 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), where it reads 'A man will find that as he alters his thoughts towards things and other people, things and other people will alter towards him.' Attributing the combined text to Allen alone is wrong; the two halves should be separated or the Marcus Aurelius line dropped.
results.suggested_reattribution: Composite: sentence 1 Marcus Aurelius (Meditations); sentence 2 James Allen (As a Man Thinketh, 1903)

results.notes: Consistently attributed to James Allen and fully consistent with the argument of 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), but I cannot confirm that this exact aphorism appears there rather than in one of his other volumes ('The Path of Prosperity', 'Above Life's Turmoil') or in a later paraphrase of his ideas. Its neat antithetical shape is typical of summary lines that get condensed out of longer passages, so I am not asserting a citation.

Widely and consistently attributed to James Allen, usually to 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), and the desire/aspiration contrast is squarely his. As with the companion line, I cannot confirm the exact volume or wording — the commonly seen form uses a semicolon, 'as small as your controlling desire; as great as your dominant aspiration' — so no print citation is asserted.

results.earliest_print_source: As a Man Thinketh, James Allen, 1903
results.notes: The author and source in the input are correct, but the wording is a variant. The original line in the 'Visions and Ideals' chapter of 'As a Man Thinketh' reads 'The dreamers are the saviours of the world.' 'Redeemers' is a later substitution. Recommend restoring 'saviours' (or 'saviors') to match the 1903 text; the attribution itself is sound.

I believe this is authentic James Baldwin — the cadence, the semicolon construction, and the moral argument are unmistakably his essayistic voice, and it is generally cited to his early-1960s essays, most often 'Nobody Knows My Name' (1961). I cannot confirm the specific essay or page, so no citation is asserted. Note this is the same person as q_0775's 'James Baldwin'; the corpus should normalize the author name across both.

This closely tracks a well-known line by the British travel writer Freya Stark, usually quoted as 'There can be no happiness if the things we believe in are different from the things we do', associated with her writing collected in 'The Journey's Echo'. The version here is a loose reworded form credited to the self-help author James Arthur Ray. I am confident the underlying thought is Stark's; recommend reattributing and restoring her wording, or dropping the quote.

Consistent with James Arthur Ray's prosperity-teaching material ('Harmonic Wealth', 2008) and with the seminar idiom of that genre, but I cannot place it in a specific book or talk. Worth flagging for editorial reasons independent of provenance: Ray was convicted of negligent homicide following the 2009 Sedona sweat-lodge deaths, which the corpus owner may wish to weigh before promoting quotes under his name.

I cannot place this in James Baldwin's essays, novels, or interviews, and the flat inspirational-poster phrasing is unlike his prose, which is dense, ironic, and syntactically complex. The name 'James Baldwin' attracts unsourced uplift of this kind. I have no candidate true author, so no reattribution is proposed — but the attribution should be treated as unsupported.

Circulates in motivational quote compilations attributed to 'James G. Bilkey,' a figure I cannot place with any biographical certainty — no book, speech, or article of his that I know of. The attribution is consistent across quote sites but that is echo, not evidence. No primary source in my knowledge.

'James King' is too common a name to anchor an attribution, and I have no recall of this line in any identifiable work. It reads like generic late-20th-century self-help prose. Honest answer: I don't know who wrote it.

Contested attribution. This line is far more commonly attributed to Peter F. Drucker in management literature than to 'James Levin,' and I cannot verify either. I have no primary Drucker source for it, so I am not asserting a reattribution — but the 'James Levin' credit is the minority claim and should be treated as weak. Flag for human review.

James Oppenheim (1882-1932) was a real American poet and novelist (best known for 'Bread and Roses'), and this line is consistently credited to him across quotation collections, which is mildly reassuring. But I cannot place it in any specific poem, novel, or essay of his, and the consistency may just reflect a single anthology entry copied forward.

There is a James Thornton (environmental lawyer and author) who wrote 'A Field Guide to the Soul' (1999), and the vocabulary here — soul, untroubled stream, one substance — would fit that book. That is inference from style, not recall of the passage, so I am not recording it as a source. Attribution unconfirmed.

Plausibly Jay-Z — the register matches his memoir 'Decoded' (2010), which contains extended reflection on artists and perception, and he has spoken this way about Basquiat in interviews. But I cannot locate this exact passage in 'Decoded' or in a specific interview from memory, so I will not cite it.

Consistently attributed to Jean Shinoda Bolen and most often traced to 'The Tao of Psychology: Synchronicity and the Self' (1979). The 'path with heart' framing is Bolen engaging Castaneda's Don Juan, which fits that book's argument well. I have moderate recall of the association but not of the page or exact edition, so I am leaving the print source null rather than manufacturing a citation.

The 'I think that...' opener and the conversational cadence suggest a spoken interview rather than a book, which would fit Bolen's many magazine interviews (Common Boundary, New Dimensions, etc.). The content is consonant with her work on soul and Jungian psychology, but I cannot identify the specific interview or book, so the attribution stands unverified.

Widely and consistently credited to Basquiat and entirely in keeping with his documented hostility to critics. It most likely comes from one of his early-1980s interviews (the Henry Geldzahler conversation in Interview magazine, 1983, is the usual candidate), but I cannot confirm which interview, so no citation is recorded.

A popular English condensation rather than a translated Sartre sentence. The authentic Sartre formulation is 'L'important n'est pas ce qu'on fait de nous, mais ce que nous faisons nous-meme de ce qu'on a fait de nous' — what matters is not what has been made of us but what we make of what has been made of us — from 'Saint Genet' (1952) and echoed in 'Search for a Method' (1957). The idea is genuinely Sartre's; this exact aphoristic wording is not traceable to him. Use with care if quoted as his words.

The author's name is misspelled in the corpus: the US diplomat and political scientist was Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (not Jeanne). The line is commonly credited to her and matches her realist idiom from the UN ambassadorship years, but I cannot place it in a specific speech, column, or book. Correct the spelling regardless of the provenance verdict.

I have no knowledge of 'Jeff Esper' as an author or speaker, and no recall of this line anywhere. It has the shape of a filler entry in a bulk quote database. I don't know who wrote it.
'Jeffrey Leaver' is not an author I can identify, and I have no recall of this line in print. Attractive phrasing, untraceable origin — the honest verdict is that I don't know.

Standard attribution to Lady Randolph Churchill (Jennie Jerome Churchill, 1854-1921), and it appears in older printed quotation dictionaries rather than only in modern web lists, which is a point in its favor. Her memoir 'The Reminiscences of Lady Randolph Churchill' (1908) is the plausible origin but I cannot confirm the passage. Note: not Winston Churchill — worth guarding against downstream drift, given Churchill's status as a misattribution magnet.

Jerry Gillies is a real author ('Moneylove,' 1978; 'Psychological Immunity'), and the attribution is consistent across quote collections. I cannot locate the line in a specific book of his, and the evidence is entirely secondary.

Genuinely Jessica Hische, the lettering artist and designer — this is her best-known line and the seed of her coinage 'procrastiworking.' It spread from her own site and talks around 2011 and she has repeated and been credited for it publicly many times, with no competing claimant. A living author with an uncontested claim is about as strong as secondary evidence gets; I lack an exact first-publication date, so no print citation.
'Jim Allen' is unidentifiable as an author here, and I have no recall of this aphorism in any source. Unknown origin.

The cadence — the list of parallel conditionals, 'the labor that works miracles' — is characteristically Jim Rohn's seminar delivery, and the attribution is consistent. But Rohn's material lives mostly in recorded seminars and later transcript compilations, so a specific book and date are hard to fix, and I cannot supply one.

A signature Jim Rohn formulation; 'whatever good things we build end up building us' is one of his most-repeated lines and is uncontested in attribution. It is usually cited from his seminar material and the compilation 'The Treasury of Quotes' (1994), but since Rohn's aphorisms were spoken first and printed later, I cannot fix a first appearance and am not recording a citation.

Consistently attributed to Joan Baez and usually traced to her 1968 memoir 'Daybreak,' whose fragmentary, confessional style fits this line well. I have moderate recall of that association but not of the passage itself, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting it.

A well-known Baez line, uncontested in attribution and one she has repeated across decades of interviews and activist speeches — it functions almost as a personal motto. No competing claimant that I know of. I cannot name the first documented utterance, so no citation is recorded.

Consonant with Joan Borysenko's mind-body work ('Minding the Body, Mending the Mind,' 1987), and I know of no competing attribution, but I cannot place this sentence in a specific book or article of hers. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

Strongly in Borysenko's voice and squarely in the territory of 'Guilt Is the Teacher, Love Is the Lesson' (1990) and 'Fire in the Soul' (1993). That is a thematic match, not a located passage, so I am not recording either as the source. Attribution plausible but unverified.

Ubiquitous in design-quote roundups credited to 'Joe Sparano,' a graphic designer, but I cannot identify a talk, article, book, or interview where he said it, nor much about him beyond the quote itself. This is the classic profile of an attribution that propagated through listicles from a single unsourced entry. Treat with suspicion despite its familiarity.

A German original circulates alongside the English ('Denken ist leicht, handeln schwer, handeln nach Gedanken das Unbequemste auf der Welt'), which is a good sign the line is genuinely Goethe's rather than an English-language invention. My recollection places it in the Wilhelm Meister material / Maximen und Reflexionen, but I cannot confirm the exact work or locus, so I am not naming one. Attribution consistent and long-standing; the specific citation is what is missing.

Circulates widely in gratitude and creativity anthologies attributed to Goethe, and a German rendering also circulates, but I cannot place it in any Goethe work, letter, or conversation I know. The imagery ('with fire or sword') is plausible for Goethe but equally plausible as a loose translation or an anthology-era paraphrase. No source named; honest uncertainty.

I recognize the German line 'Sobald du dir vertraust, sobald weisst du zu leben' and associate it with Faust, Part One (1808), spoken by Mephistopheles. I am confident enough in the German original to call the Goethe attribution sound, but not confident enough in the exact scene or line number to print a citation, so earliest_print_source is left null rather than guessed.

John Balguy (1686-1748), English divine, is the standard attribution, and the line appears in nineteenth-century compilations such as Tryon Edwards' A Dictionary of Thoughts. But dictionary-of-quotations attributions of that era are frequently unsourced or laundered, and I cannot place this sentence in any of Balguy's own writings (Divine Rectitude, the Foundation of Moral Goodness, etc.). Consistently attributed to the American novelist John Berry, and my recollection associates it with his novel Flight of White Crows (1961) - but I am not confident enough in that title-to-quote link to print it as a citation. Well established as Cage's, from his interviews and conversations rather than a formal essay - I associate it with the interview literature (Kostelanetz's Conversing with Cage, or the For the Birds conversations with Daniel Charles). AUTHOR NAME ERROR: there is no 'John Christian Bovee'. Attributed with fair consistency to John D. Rockefeller Jr. in philanthropy and fundraising literature, and the sentiment matches his public statements on giving. But I cannot connect it to a specific speech, letter, or his often-quoted 'I Believe' credo, and short uplift lines in fundraising materials are a common site of drift. Attribution plausible, source unverified.

Always credited to 'John E. Southard' and effectively never to anyone else, but I know nothing about who Southard was and can find no work, publication, or date associated with him in my training knowledge. Authentic Kennedy in substance and phrasing; he returned repeatedly to the George Bernard Shaw line 'I dream things that never were and say why not' (Back to Methuselah), most famously in his address to the Irish Parliament, 28 June 1963. If promoted, either restore the original or mark it as adapted.

Authentic Kennedy from his set of remarks on the arts and national culture. My recollection points to either the Amherst College address honoring Robert Frost (26 October 1963) or his remarks for the National Cultural Center (1962); both are real speeches with closely related language, and I cannot tell which contains this sentence. Attributed to Dulles with fair consistency in management and leadership literature, but I cannot tie it to any speech, dispatch, or writing of his. The formulation reads more like postwar business-book aphorism than diplomatic prose, which raises the possibility that a management author coined or reshaped it and the Dulles name attached later. No evidence of a specific alternate author, so no reattribution suggested.

Cannot place this passage. 'John Gray' is ambiguous: the self-help author of Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus and What You Feel, You Can Heal; the political philosopher (Straw Dogs); and others. The therapeutic register suggests the self-help John Gray, but the specific argument (that removing another's pain removes their growth) is a commonplace of pastoral-care and codependency writing and could belong to several authors. Unverified on both source and which John Gray.

Two problems. (1) The core sentence, 'Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success...', appears in nineteenth-century quotation dictionaries credited to Keats, but I cannot locate it in his letters or poems, and the reasoning about 'discovery of what is false' is uncharacteristically didactic-empiricist for Keats. (2) The opening two sentences ('Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience.') read as a modern motivational preamble grafted onto the older sentence - flat, contemporary diction unlike the rest. Recommend not promoting; at minimum strip the prepended sentences.

The attribution is broadly sound - Kennedy did use this line in campaign-era speeches (I associate it with his 1959-60 addresses, including a United Negro College Fund speech in Indianapolis, April 1959) - but two things should block promotion. (1) FACTUALLY FALSE: the etymology is wrong. Sinologist Victor Mair has repeatedly debunked it; the second character in weiji is ji, meaning incipient moment or crux, not 'opportunity'. (2) NOT ORIGINAL: the trope predates Kennedy in English-language missionary writing on China (Quote Investigator traces it to the late 1930s), so he popularized rather than coined it. Also note the author field reads 'John Kennedy'; should be 'John F. Kennedy'. Recommend rejection on accuracy grounds even though the speaker is real.

I have no reliable knowledge of John MacEnulty as a published author and cannot locate this passage in anything I know. The content is a restatement of the Heraclitean river commonplace ('You cannot step in the same stream twice') wrapped in contemporary mindfulness language, which makes independent verification harder rather than easier. No source, no date, no corroborating attribution. Honest answer is that I do not know.

Genuine Maeda - the design/art distinction is one of his recurring formulations, expressed in his talks, interviews, and writing (including his TED remarks on art, technology and design). Contemporary and well documented as his, but I cannot pin the first appearance to a specific book, post, or talk transcript, so no citation is printed. Attribution itself is not in question.
