A well-known Gibran aphorism, in the paradoxical two-clause form typical of Sand and Foam (1926), where I believe it appears. Attribution to Gibran is consistent and I have no evidence pointing elsewhere; I withhold the print citation because I cannot confirm the volume.

Karen Sunde is a real American playwright, and this line circulates in quotation dictionaries under her name, but I cannot connect it to any of her plays, essays, or interviews. Short aphorisms of this kind in quote compilations frequently carry unsourced attributions. Attribution is plausible but effectively untraceable from what I know.

Authentically Jaspersian in both content and translation register -- 'self-being' is the standard English rendering of Selbstsein in E. B. Ashton's translation of Jaspers, and the claim that refusing communication betrays both other and self is central to Jaspers's account of existential communication in Philosophie (1932), vol. 2 (Existenzerhellung). I believe that is the source but cannot confirm the volume or page, so I leave the citation field null rather than assert it.

This is the best-known line associated with the German Zen teacher and psychotherapist Karlfried Graf Durckheim (Graf Karlfried von Durckheim-Montmartin), and it matches his central theme of transformation through the 'exercise' of dying to the ego; it is usually cited from The Way of Transformation, though I cannot confirm that locus. The author field is garbled: 'Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim' should read 'Karlfried Graf Durckheim' ('Graf' is the German title Count, not a given name). Flagged as a name correction, not a change of author.

Consistently attributed to Katharine Hepburn and entirely in character for her public persona, but I cannot trace it to her memoir Me: Stories of My Life (1991), to a documented interview, or to any dated source. Short, quotable lines attached to famous personalities are a standard misattribution pattern, so I keep this below the promotion bar despite the consistency of the attribution.

Katherine Paterson is a real and much-quoted author (Bridge to Terabithia; two-time Newbery winner) who wrote and spoke often on peace, difference, and empathy, so the attribution is plausible and probably comes from a speech, acceptance address, or essay collection such as Gates of Excellence or A Sense of Wonder. I cannot identify the specific occasion or text.

I have no knowledge of Kathleen A. Sutton and cannot place her or this sentence. The sentiment is a commonplace that appears in many forms across proverb collections and self-help writing, which makes a single named originator unlikely to be verifiable. Honest answer: source unknown.

Ken Hakuta is the Wacky WallWalker marketer known as 'Dr. Fad,' and the line fits his self-presentation and his 1988 book on inventing fads; it is consistently attributed to him in business-quote collections. I cannot confirm a book, article, or interview as the origin, so the attribution stays unverified.

Widely and consistently attributed to Ken Kesey, and the phrasing and stance match his interview voice; it appears to come from a spoken interview rather than his published fiction. I cannot identify the interview, outlet, or year, and spoken-source quotes of this kind often drift in wording, so I hold this at unverified despite the consistency of the attribution.

A signature Ken Keyes Jr. formulation; 'everyone you meet is your mirror' is one of the phrases most closely associated with him and with Handbook to Higher Consciousness (1972), where I believe the passage appears. Attribution to Keyes is consistent and I know of no competing claimant, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so I leave the print source null.

Consistent with Ken Wilber's recurring argument that ego-fighting is itself an ego project, a point he makes in No Boundary and in the One Taste journals, and the paradoxical compression is his style. I cannot place this exact sentence in a specific book, and similar formulations circulate in Advaita and Zen teaching contexts, so the wording may be a paraphrase of Wilber rather than a direct quotation.

Attributed consistently to Keshavan Nair, and the content -- courage as the ground of integrity, joined to compassion and humility -- matches the argument of his A Higher Standard of Leadership: Lessons from the Life of Gandhi (1994), which is the likely source. I cannot confirm the passage in that book, so I do not assert the citation.

A widely circulated Gibran line whose triadic structure and tone are genuinely his; it is often traced to his Arabic-period writings in English translation (collections such as A Tear and a Smile / The Broken Wings tradition) rather than to The Prophet. Because the translation source is unsettled and translated aphorisms are prone to drift, I keep this at attributed without a citation. Author spelling should be normalized to 'Kahlil Gibran' for consistency with q_0860 through q_0863 in this batch.

Enormously widespread attribution to J. Krishnamurti, and consistent with his recurring theme that conformity to a diseased society is not sanity. However, I cannot place this exact sentence in any of his published books or transcribed talks. The wording has the compressed, aphoristic feel of a later condensation of a longer passage rather than a verbatim line. Some circulating versions cite 'Commentaries on Living' but the passages there differ. Honest verdict: attribution is plausible and near-universal, verbatim sourcing is absent from my knowledge.

I cannot place this five-word line anywhere in Krishnamurti's corpus. It gestures at a real Krishnamurti theme (judgment/evaluation as an obstacle to seeing, cf. his 'observing without evaluating' formulations), but the phrasing is not one I recognize from his talks or books. Reads like a social-media compression of his ideas. No traceable source.

This is a genuine and central Krishnamurti formulation, not a paraphrase. 'The thinker is the thought' belongs to his signature family of identity statements alongside 'the observer is the observed' and 'the experiencer is the experience,' and it recurs across his 1950s-era writing and talks (it is discussed at length in works of that period such as 'The First and Last Freedom' and the 'Commentaries on Living' series). I am confident in the attribution but am not able to confirm a specific page or dated talk from memory, so I leave the print field null rather than guess a citation.

Genuine Krishnamurti prose in both cadence and vocabulary ('this extraordinary thing called love'; 'the world is transformed'), and my recollection places it in his discussion of love in 'Freedom from the Known' (1969). I am confident enough in the attribution to Krishnamurti to sit at 0.80, but not confident enough in the exact book and chapter to record a print citation, so that field stays null. Circulating versions vary slightly in punctuation.

results.earliest_print_source: Land of the Spotted Eagle, Luther Standing Bear, 1933
results.notes: Not an anonymous proverb. This is a lightly reworded line from Luther Standing Bear (Oglala Lakota), whose 'Land of the Spotted Eagle' (1933) contains the passage rendered as 'Man's heart, away from nature, becomes hard.' The 'Lakota proverb' label is the usual folk-anonymization of a named Native author, which strips him of credit. Confidence figure reflects the weak 'Lakota proverb' attribution; my confidence in the Standing Bear reattribution is considerably higher (~0.7), though the corpus wording is a paraphrase rather than his exact sentence.

Lama Surya Das is a real American Dzogchen teacher and author ('Awakening the Buddha Within,' 1997), and the sentiment fits his register, but I cannot locate this four-word aphorism in any of his books or talks that I know. It is also generic enough to have many independent authors. No traceable source.

Lance Secretan is a real leadership author ('Reclaiming Higher Ground,' 1997; 'Inspirational Leadership,' 1999) and this passage matches his documented thesis that leadership is an inspirational and heart-centered human activity rather than a technique or process. The length and paragraph structure suggest it was excerpted from one of his books, which raises my confidence in the attribution above the floor. But I cannot identify which book or confirm the wording, so no citation is recorded.

results.earliest_print_source: "Dreams," Langston Hughes, first published 1922; collected in The Dream Keeper and Other Poems, 1932
results.notes: From Langston Hughes's short poem 'Dreams.' The verse lines read: 'Hold fast to dreams / For if dreams die / Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly.' The corpus entry runs the lines together as prose and adds a comma after 'dreams' and drops the hyphen in 'broken-winged'; consider restoring the line breaks and the hyphen if the corpus preserves verse formatting. Attribution itself is certain.

Does not correspond to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching in the standard translations I know (Legge, Waley, Feng/English, Mitchell, Lau, Addiss/Lombardo). The English is modern and idiomatic ('flow as life flows'), characteristic of the large body of free-floating pseudo-Lao Tzu circulating online. It may be a loose New Age rendering distantly inspired by the water imagery of ch. 8 or ch. 78, but I cannot connect it to a source text or a named translator.

results.earliest_print_source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 48 (traditionally attributed to Laozi, c. 4th century BCE)
results.notes: A genuine, if loose, English rendering of Tao Te Ching ch. 48: 為學日益，為道日損 — 'in the pursuit of learning, every day something is gained; in the pursuit of the Way, every day something is dropped.' The paraphrase substitutes 'wisdom' for the Tao and 'remove things' for the subtractive 損, so it is not a scholarly translation, but the thought and structure are authentically from the text. Standard caveat: Laozi's historical existence and sole authorship of the Tao Te Ching are traditional rather than established.

Not in the Tao Te Ching. No chapter treats time as a 'created thing,' and the register — a self-help reframe about scheduling and willingness, complete with quoted colloquial speech ('I don't have time') — is unmistakably modern American. This circulates heavily in productivity writing as Lao Tzu, which is a textbook case of a modern maxim borrowing an ancient name for authority. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I offer no reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 (traditionally attributed to Laozi, c. 4th century BCE)
results.notes: Genuine. Tao Te Ching ch. 64: 千里之行，始於足下, literally 'a journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.' 'With a single step' is a translator's idiomatic choice rather than the literal sense, and the shift is worth noting because the Chinese emphasizes where one already stands rather than the act of stepping. The attribution to the Tao Te Ching is not in doubt; Laozi's historical authorship is traditional.

results.earliest_print_source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 17 (traditionally attributed to Laozi, c. 4th century BCE)
results.notes: A modern managerial paraphrase built on genuine material. Tao Te Ching ch. 17 ranks rulers — the best barely known, then loved and praised, then feared, then despised — and closes 功成事遂，百姓皆謂我自然, commonly rendered 'when the work is done, the people say we did it ourselves.' The corpus wording compresses and reorders that into a three-tier leadership maxim; this formulation is popular in leadership literature (John Heider's 'The Tao of Leadership,' 1985, is one well-known vehicle for such renderings) and is not a translation. Holding at 0.70 rather than higher because the source thought is authentic but the sentence is not Lao Tzu's.

results.earliest_print_source: Mrs. Dymond, Anne Isabella Ritchie, 1885
results.notes: Not Lao Tzu, and not a Chinese proverb. Nothing resembling it appears in the Tao Te Ching. The earliest known form traced by quotation researchers is in Anne Isabella Ritchie's novel 'Mrs. Dymond' (1885): 'if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour; if you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.' The saying has since been variously credited to Lao Tzu, Maimonides, and Confucius, all without support. Confidence value reflects the Lao Tzu attribution, which I regard as clearly wrong; my confidence in the Ritchie origin is high (~0.8).
results.suggested_reattribution: Anne Isabella Ritchie (Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie), Mrs. Dymond, 1885

results.notes: I cannot match this triad to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching. Its parallel structure faintly echoes ch. 8, which lists virtues by domain ('in dwelling, be close to the land; in dealing with others, be gentle and kind; in speech, be true...'), but that passage does not repeat 'kindness' and does not produce 'confidence,' 'profoundness,' or 'love' as outcomes. 'Profoundness' in particular is not a word that appears in any translation I know. Most likely a modern reworking that drifted far enough from ch. 8 to count as a separate composition. Attribution to Lao Tzu is weak.

I cannot place this in the Tao Te Ching or in the Zhuangzi. The sentiment is broadly Daoist in flavor (equanimity toward fortune and misfortune, cf. the reversals of ch. 58), but the archaic-sounding English construction 'Seek not... and be not' suggests a paraphraser imitating scriptural diction rather than a translation of a specific line. No traceable source.

Not in the Tao Te Ching. This is one of the most heavily circulated pseudo-Lao Tzu lines on the internet, and the usual form is 'Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength, while loving someone deeply gives you courage' — note that the corpus version has the two clauses swapped, so it is a garbled variant of an already baseless attribution. Even the standard form has no identified author. Recommend removal or reattribution to 'Anonymous' if kept.

I cannot find this sentence in Tao Te Ching translations. There is a real thematic neighbor in ch. 52, 見小曰明 ('seeing the small is called clarity/insight'), and ch. 64's counsel to deal with things while they are still latent, so a very free paraphrase is conceivable. But 'genius' is a European category alien to the text's vocabulary, which argues for a Western aphorist's composition later hung on Lao Tzu's name. Weak attribution.

Consistently attributed to Larry Eisenberg across quotation collections, and the attribution has been stable long enough that it is unlikely to be pure invention. Complicating factor: at least two public figures share the name (the science-fiction writer and short-story author, and a clergyman), and I cannot determine which is meant or identify an originating publication. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

Very widely attributed to Lena Horne, often loosely to an interview in her later career, and the attribution is stable and specific enough to take seriously. However, I cannot confirm a primary source, and proverbial formulations of the same idea (it is not the burden but the manner of carrying it) circulated before her. Plausible that she said it and gave it currency rather than originated it. Below the promotion bar until a primary source is found.

Consistently and specifically credited to Leo Burnett throughout advertising literature, where his speeches and internal memos are unusually well preserved and were collected posthumously (notably in '100 LEO's: Wit and Wisdom from Leo Burnett,' 1995). The hedged, conversational phrasing — 'I think,' 'is still' — reads like transcribed speech rather than a manufactured aphorism, which supports authenticity. I cannot confirm the specific speech or page, so no citation is recorded and this sits just below the promotion bar.

Matches Leo Buscaglia's documented themes and first-person-plural style, and my sense is that it comes from his writing on self-determination, plausibly 'Personhood' (1978). Attribution is widespread and I have no reason to doubt it, but I cannot identify the book or confirm the wording, and Buscaglia's popularity means his name attracts unsourced uplift. Recording as unverified.

Consistent with Buscaglia's central subject and voice; likely from 'Love' (1972) or 'Living, Loving and Learning' (1982), but I cannot confirm which or verify the wording. Attribution is widespread and plausible rather than evidenced. Same caveat as q_0897: his name is a magnet for unsourced sentiment about love.

results.earliest_print_source: The Marketing Imagination, Theodore Levitt, 1983 (quoting Leo McGinneva)
results.notes: The attribution is correct and unusually well documented for a line of this kind. Theodore Levitt credited Leo McGinneva by name for this formulation in 'The Marketing Imagination' (1983), where it appears in his discussion of what customers actually buy; Levitt's own better-known paraphrase is 'people don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole.' So McGinneva is the originator and Levitt the transmitter — this corpus entry has it right, which is worth noting since the line is far more often credited to Levitt. Note the text uses a typographic apostrophe in 'don't'.

Attributed to Tolstoy almost universally and for a long time, which gives it more weight than a recent internet attribution, but I cannot locate it in his works. It is not a line I can place in 'What Is Art?' (1897), his major statement on the subject, and it may originate in a letter, a diary entry, a recorded conversation, or a secondary account — or in a translator's compression of a longer passage. Also note the author name is spelled 'Leo Tolstoi'; the corpus should probably normalize to the standard 'Leo Tolstoy.' Attribution plausible, sourcing unconfirmed.

Tolstoy was a committed vegetarian from 1885 and argued exactly this in his 1892 essay 'The First Step' (Pervaya stupen), written as a preface to the Russian edition of Howard Williams's 'The Ethics of Diet'. The usual circulating wording is 'A man can live and be healthy without killing animals for food; therefore, if he eats meat, he participates in taking animal life merely for the sake of his appetite' — the corpus text is a gender-neutralized paraphrase of that. I cannot place the sentence at a specific page or confirm it is a direct translation rather than a summary of his argument, so I am not asserting a primary source. Attribution to Tolstoy is consistent across sources and entirely in character; the exact provenance is not.

Consistently attributed to Leonard Nimoy across quote collections and often cited alongside his poetry (he published several volumes, e.g. 'You & I', 1973, and 'Warmed by Love'). The sentiment and the aphoristic style fit his published verse. I cannot place it in a specific book, poem, interview, or speech from my training knowledge, and it may be a line lifted from a longer poem. No competing attribution that I know of, so the author is plausible but unverified.

This is a well-known false attribution. The line does not appear anywhere in Leonardo's notebooks or the Trattato della Pittura, and the Italian version circulating online ('La semplicita e l'ultima sofisticazione') is a back-translation from English, which is itself strong evidence of modern origin. Wikiquote lists it under Leonardo's disputed/misattributed section. Its popularity comes largely from twentieth-century advertising use, notably the 1977 Apple II brochure, where it appeared as a tagline. I do not reliably know the true earliest coiner, so I am not naming one rather than guessing.

results.earliest_print_source: The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci, Dmitry Merezhkovsky, 1900 (Russian; English translation 1902)
results.notes: A documented case of fiction laundered into a quotation. The 'time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they now look upon the murder of men' line comes from Dmitry Merezhkovsky's historical novel 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' (1900), where it is dialogue invented for the character of Leonardo. It appears in no surviving Leonardo manuscript. Leonardo's actual vegetarianism is separately evidenced — chiefly Andrea Corsali's 1515 letter to Giuliano de' Medici describing him as eating no meat — but that is not this sentence. Wikiquote files it as misattributed.
results.suggested_reattribution: Dmitry Merezhkovsky (fictional dialogue in 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci', 1900)

results.earliest_print_source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci / Trattato della Pittura; English ed. Jean Paul Richter, 1883
results.notes: This is genuine Leonardo, from the painting precepts collected in the Trattato della Pittura and reproduced in the standard notebook editions (Richter 1883; MacCurdy 1938). It appears among his instructions to painters on stepping back from work to judge it — the passage advising the painter to withdraw, since distance shrinks the work and makes disharmony of proportion visible at a glance. Translations vary in wording, and 'a lack of harmony or portion' in the corpus text looks like a corruption of 'proportion'. I am confident in the attribution but not in the precise translation lineage of this rendering, so I am holding just at the promotion bar rather than claiming primary verification.

Standard Les Brown motivational material, attributed to him consistently and without competing claimants. Most plausibly from his book 'Live Your Dreams' (1992) or his speaking material, but I cannot confirm a page or a specific talk, so I am leaving the print source null. Living-speaker quotes of this kind are rarely sourced in the aggregators that carry them; the attribution is likely right, the citation is unestablished.

Leslie Fieger is a New Thought / self-development author known for the DELFIN Knowledge System trilogy. Quotes attributed to him circulate almost exclusively through quotation aggregators and mailing-list signatures rather than through cited books. I have no independent knowledge of this line in any of his published texts and cannot confirm or refute it. Low-profile author means low misattribution risk but also no verification path from training knowledge.

Same situation as the other Fieger line. The vocabulary — conscious mind directing subconscious mind into harmony with universal mind — is squarely the New Thought idiom of Fieger's DELFIN material, so the attribution is stylistically plausible. I cannot place it in a specific book or lesson and will not invent one. No competing attribution known.

A signature Tomlin one-liner, attributed to her with great consistency. Important caveat: the great majority of Lily Tomlin's stage and television material was written by Jane Wagner, her longtime collaborator and later spouse, so 'Lily Tomlin said it' often means 'Jane Wagner wrote it and Lily Tomlin performed it'. I cannot determine which show or special this line came from, so I cannot say whether Wagner authored this specific joke. Attribution to Tomlin as speaker is safe; attribution as author is not.

Widely and consistently attributed to Lily Tomlin, and I believe it belongs to the Trudy the bag lady material from 'The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe' (Broadway, 1985) — the same show that produced 'Reality is nothing but a collective hunch'. If that placement is right, the written author is Jane Wagner, who wrote the entire show; Tomlin performed it. I am not confident enough in the placement to state the show as a source or to file a formal reattribution, but the Wagner authorship question should be flagged before this is promoted.

results.earliest_print_source: Afterthoughts, Logan Pearsall Smith, 1931
results.notes: Genuine and well sourced. From Smith's aphorism collection 'Afterthoughts' (1931), in the 'Life and Human Nature' section. The original reads 'There are two things to aim at in life: first, to get what you want; and, after that, to enjoy it. Only the wisest of mankind achieve the second.' Two alterations in the corpus text: 'mankind' has been changed to 'humankind', and 'achieve' to 'has achieved'. Recommend restoring the original wording, since a modernized quotation that is still presented as a quotation is a small falsification.

results.earliest_print_source: Don Juan, Canto III, stanza 3, Lord Byron, 1821
results.notes: Genuine Byron, from Don Juan, Canto III, stanza 3. The verse line is 'In her first passion woman loves her lover, / In all the others all she loves is love'. The corpus text flattens the second line to 'she loves love', losing both the meter and the point of the antithesis. Recommend restoring the original couplet.

results.earliest_print_source: Letters to His Son, Philip Dormer Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield, letter of 26 December 1749 (published 1774)
results.notes: Genuine Chesterfield, from the celebrated letter to his son on the use of time, dated 26 December 1749 Old Style and published in the 1774 collection 'Letters to His Son'. The original opens 'Know the true value of time' — the corpus text has dropped 'true'. Original punctuation is 'no procrastination: never put off till to-morrow what you can do to-day.' The 'never put off till tomorrow' proverb long predates Chesterfield and is not his coinage; he is quoting a commonplace inside a sentence that is his own.

I have no knowledge of Loren Fincher as an author, speaker, or public figure, and no knowledge of this line from any published source. It has the cadence of inspirational-newsletter or greeting-card writing and circulates, as far as I can tell, only through quote aggregators. Cannot confirm the person exists as attributed, cannot identify a real author, and will not guess. This is an honest 'I don't know'.

Genuine Kahn in substance, but two corrections are needed. First, the author's name is misspelled in the corpus: it is Louis I. Kahn (1901-1974), not 'Louis Khan'. Second, Kahn's formulation is plural — 'Architecture is the thoughtful making of spaces' — and it opens his contribution to Perspecta 4 (Yale architectural journal, 1957), continuing 'It is the creating of spaces that evoke a feeling of appropriate use.' I am confident of the sentence and of Kahn as its author; I am less certain of the exact issue and year, so I have left the print source null rather than risk a wrong citation. Fix the surname regardless of promotion outcome.
results.suggested_reattribution: Louis I. Kahn (spelling correction, not a change of author)

results.notes: Attributed to Louis L'Amour consistently and with no competing claimant. The most likely home is his memoir 'Education of a Wandering Man' (1989), which contains extended reflection on reading, writing, and how the mind works on problems below awareness — but I cannot confirm the sentence is in that book, so I am not citing it as a source. The observation is characteristic of his prose about the writing craft. Plausible author, unestablished citation.

Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently, apparently originating in a magazine interview in which she described her 'everyday religion'. Note for the corpus editor: this is a truncated duplicate of q_0924, which carries the fuller and more likely original form beginning 'I have an everyday religion that works for me.' One of the two should be dropped, and the fuller version is the better record. Attribution plausible; no primary citation available to me.

Widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the context of interviewers asking how she developed her physical comedy. The sentiment matches her documented account of learning comedy as craft rather than possessing it as a gift. I cannot place it in a specific interview, and it may derive from her posthumously published autobiography 'Love, Lucy' (1996), but I will not cite that without confirmation. No competing attribution known.

results.earliest_print_source: 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', James Baldwin, New York Times Book Review, 14 January 1962
results.notes: This is James Baldwin, not Lucille Ball, and the misattribution is not close. The line comes from Baldwin's 1962 New York Times Book Review essay 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', on the responsibilities of American writers; it is one of his most frequently quoted sentences and is well documented in Baldwin scholarship and collections. It has nothing to do with Ball, and the corpus has additionally filed it under 'humor', which compounds the error. Strong recommendation: reattribute to Baldwin or drop.

A vaudeville-era stock gag about guessing a woman's age, of the kind that circulates freely and attaches itself to whichever comedian is being quoted. It is attributed to Lucille Ball in aggregators but I have no evidence she originated it, and jokes of this shape predate her career. Weak attribution; I cannot name a true originator, which is typical for anonymous stage material.

Reads as genuine first-person interview material rather than a manufactured aphorism, and the content matches the documented arc of Ball's early years as a contract player in Hollywood before her success. That specificity is mild evidence of authenticity — invented quotes rarely include this kind of ordinary biographical detail. Still, I cannot identify the interview or publication, so the citation is unestablished.

A free-floating domestic quip attributed to Lucille Ball in quote collections. I have no source for it and no strong reason to think it originated with her; observations of this form are common in mid-century newspaper humor columns and get reassigned to famous names. Weak attribution, no identifiable origin.

Consistently attributed to Lucille Ball and structured like genuine transcribed interview speech — the self-interrupting 'Luck? I don't know anything about luck' opening, the correction mid-thought, the dash. Manufactured quotations tend to be smoother than this. The sentiment also matches her well-documented insistence that her career came from work rather than fortune. I cannot identify the interview, so no citation.

The fuller and probably original form of the line duplicated at q_0917; the 'I have an everyday religion that works for me' opening is the part that usually gets trimmed off in circulation, and its presence here suggests this version is closer to the source. Attributed to Ball consistently, apparently from a magazine interview. I cannot identify the publication. Recommend keeping this version and dropping q_0917. Also note it is filed under 'humor' but is not a joke — the category looks wrong.

Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently across collections, with the reflective interview cadence of her later-career remarks about resilience in show business. No competing attribution known to me and nothing suspicious about it, but also no traceable source — I cannot name an interview, article, or book. Plausible but uncited. Like several others in this run it is filed under 'humor' despite being straightforwardly earnest.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the form 'I'd rather regret the things I've done than regret the things I haven't done.' I cannot place a primary interview, memoir passage, or dated print appearance from training knowledge. The sentiment also belongs to a large family of older 'regret what you didn't do' maxims (compare the apocryphal Twain 'Twenty years from now' line), which raises the baseline risk that this was retrofitted onto a famous name. Plausible but unverified.

The IDEA is genuinely Lucretian: De Rerum Natura I.313 has 'stilicidi casus lapidem cavat' — the fall of dripping water hollows the stone. But this specific English wording, with the 'not by violence, but by oft falling' antithesis, is not a standard translation of that line; I recall it as English homiletic phrasing associated with Hugh Latimer's mid-16th-century preaching ('the drop of rain maketh a hole in the stone, not by violence, but by oft falling'). Related but distinct is Ovid's 'gutta cavat lapidem' (Ex Ponto IV.10.5). So the attribution is half-right: Lucretius for the thought, an English preacher's rhetoric for the sentence. Flagging rather than reattributing because my recall of the Latimer wording is good but not certain.

I recall a remark of this shape in Wittgenstein's Culture and Value (Vermischte Bemerkungen), the posthumous collection of personal notebook remarks from the 1930s-40s, running roughly 'When you are frightened of the truth (as I am now) then it is never the whole truth that you have an inkling of.' The 'than' in the corpus text is a transcription corruption of 'that', and the ellipsis marks an elided parenthetical. I am reasonably confident the remark is authentic Wittgenstein but cannot name page or dated entry, so I am not citing a print source and am holding confidence below the promotion bar. Worth a human check against Culture and Value.

M. C. (Mary Caroline) Richards, potter and poet, wrote Centering in Pottery, Poetry, and the Person (1962), The Crossing Point, and Toward Wholeness; this aphorism is stylistically consistent with her work and with Centering's themes of self-formation through craft. I cannot place the line in a specific book or page from training knowledge, and short epigrammatic fragments like this circulate easily without provenance. Attribution is plausible and I have no evidence against it, but nothing supports it either.

This is a modern English distillation of a Buddhist teaching (the second arrow, Sallatha Sutta), not a translation of any canonical text. The 'M. Kathleen Casey' credit propagates through 20th-century recovery and daily-meditation literature and through quote aggregators, but I cannot identify a book, page, or date for it, and Casey herself is a thinly documented figure easily confused with Karen Casey (Each Day a New Beginning, Hazelden). The line was popularized in the wider culture by Haruki Murakami's What I Talk About When I Talk About Running (2007), where he presents it as an anonymous runners' mantra rather than crediting Casey. Attribution is a convention, not evidence.

Circulates under Escher's name in design and business collections, but I know a closely matching line from Miguel de Unamuno — 'Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible' / 'Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible' — which reads as the likelier origin. I cannot place the sentence in Escher's own writings (his essays and letters are fairly well documented and this is not a phrasing I associate with them). My Unamuno recall is solid on the Spanish wording but I cannot name the specific work, so the reattribution is offered as probable, not established, and the Escher attribution should not be promoted.

Macrina Wiederkehr (1939-2020), Benedictine sister and author of A Tree Full of Angels (1988), Seasons of Your Heart, and Behold Your Life. The passage is idiomatically hers — the vocabulary of blessing, presence, and daily decision matches her devotional prose — and I have no reason to doubt the attribution. But I cannot identify which of her books it comes from, and prose excerpts from devotional writers are frequently re-cut and re-punctuated by anthologists. Attribution plausible, source unplaced.

results.earliest_print_source: A Tree Full of Angels: Seeing the Holy in the Ordinary, Macrina Wiederkehr, 1988
results.notes: Strong internal evidence: the passage contains both halves of the book's own title — 'Every tree is full of angels' and the seeing-the-holy-in-the-ordinary theme — and theophany-in-the-ordinary is the organizing argument of A Tree Full of Angels (Harper & Row, 1988). This is the single most-anthologized Wiederkehr passage and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I am confident in the book but cannot give a page, and I am citing from recall rather than from a copy in front of me, so I am stopping short of 'verified'.

'Maharishi' is a title, not an author — presumably Maharishi Mahesh Yogi is intended, but the corpus entry does not say so, and the passage does not read like his teaching or like translated Indian devotional prose. The idiom is modern American therapeutic-spiritual English ('the ego searches for shortcomings', 'nothing is ever needed but more love') and sits much closer to the A Course in Miracles milieu — Jampolsky, Prather, Williamson and their imitators — than to Vedic commentary. I cannot identify the actual author, and I will not guess one. The attribution as it stands is unusable and the text should not be promoted under this name.

One of the more defensible Gandhi attributions: the sentiment is squarely his (seva as self-realization) and the line is generally treated as sourced in his writings rather than as folk attribution. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the Young India issue, so I am not citing a source. Held at 0.6 rather than higher because Gandhi is a misattribution magnet and 'widely cited with consistent wording' is weaker evidence for him than for almost any other author. Note the corpus text has a typo: 'youself' should be 'yourself'.

The form usually treated as closer to Gandhi is 'The future depends on what we do in the present.' The 'what you do today' version in the corpus is a later, punchier simplification of that, of the kind motivational-poster culture produces. I cannot place either form in a primary Gandhi text. Given how heavily Gandhi's name attracts unsourced aphorisms, and given that this specific wording appears to be a rewrite rather than the earliest form, it should not be promoted.

This is a modern condensation of q_0938 in the same batch ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be...'), which is the longer and better-documented form of the same passage. The underlying thought is authentically Gandhi's, but this compressed first-person rewrite is not his sentence. Recommend the corpus keep q_0938 and treat this as a duplicate paraphrase rather than a separate quote.

This longer form is the one that appears in serious Gandhi collections and is generally treated as sourced to his own writings, with stable wording across citations — a good sign, since spurious Gandhi lines tend to drift. The prose rhythm ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be', 'On the contrary...') is consistent with his English. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the periodical and date, so no print source is cited and I am holding just below the promotion bar. A human check against the Collected Works would likely confirm it.

This is the 'thoughts become words, words become actions, habits become values, values become destiny' chain, one of the most durable false Gandhi attributions. No Gandhi source exists for it. Its ancestor is the 19th-century English maxim 'Sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny', variously credited to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles and itself of contested origin; the modern positive-thinking chain is a 20th-century self-help reworking that later acquired Gandhi's name. I can identify the family the saying descends from but not a single true author, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing. Should not appear in the corpus under Gandhi.

Ubiquitous under Gandhi's name, especially in slow-living and productivity writing, but I cannot place it in any primary text and I associate it with the unsourced tier of the Gandhi quote literature rather than the documented tier. The epigram's shape — a single modern aphorism about 'speed' — fits mid-to-late 20th-century Western anxieties about pace more naturally than Gandhi's own idiom. Plausible in sentiment, unsupported in provenance.

The documented origin of this formula is the American pacifist A. J. Muste, who said 'There is no way to peace; peace is the way' — a line strongly associated with him in the 1960s and quoted in coverage around his death in 1967. The corpus's 'no path to peace / peace is the path' is a variant of Muste's sentence, and the Gandhi credit appears to be later drift onto a bigger name, a pattern well documented for pacifist aphorisms. I am confident enough in the Muste attribution to name it, though I cannot cite the specific speech or article.

I believe this is authentic Gandhi, from his journalism of the 1920s (the Young India period), and it is one of the Gandhi passages that circulates with a real source trail rather than as a bare aphorism. Two textual notes for the corpus: the authentic wording is 'transmuted', not 'transmitted' — the corpus text has the corruption twice, which flattens the heat/energy metaphor — and 'a power which can move the world' is the more usual ending. Recommend correcting to 'transmuted' before any promotion. Not citing a dated source because I cannot pin the issue.

Well attested by the standards of Gandhi quotation. The line comes with a consistent anecdote — Gandhi, pressed by a journalist for a message and having no time to talk, wrote 'My life is my message' on a scrap of paper — and it is established enough to have been used as the title of Narayan Desai's multi-volume Gandhi biography. I cannot fix the date or the journalist with confidence, so no print source is cited, but the attribution itself is solid.

Consistently attributed to Gandhi with stable wording, and I associate it with his own writing rather than with the aggregator tier — the balanced construction ('the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err') and the theme of humility before one's own certainty are characteristic. It appears in the standard Gandhi anthologies of the All Men Are Brothers type. I cannot name the original article or speech, so it stays below the promotion bar pending a check against the Collected Works.

The single most famous thing Gandhi never said in these words. No source exists in his writings or speeches. The genuine passage it compresses is 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him' — a different and more careful claim. The imperative-slogan wording appears to originate in 1970s American self-help; Arleen Lorrance's The Love Project material (c. 1974) carried 'Be the change you want to see happen', and the Gandhi credit attached later. Brian Morton's widely read 2011 New York Times piece 'Falser Words Were Never Spoken' laid this out. I name Lorrance as probable origin of the phrasing, but the sentiment is a fair paraphrase of Gandhi, so the corpus may prefer to carry the authentic longer passage instead. Do not promote under Gandhi as written.
results.suggested_reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi

results.notes: Extremely widely quoted — it is a fixture of animal-welfare campaigning — but I know it as one of the Gandhi lines for which no source in the Collected Works has been located, and it is commonly listed in the unsourced or disputed tier of Gandhi quotation. Related sentiments do appear in his writing on cow protection and ahimsa, which is likely how the attribution took hold. Ubiquity here is a function of the cause it serves, not of evidence.

Reads as authentic: it is long, syntactically unpolished, argumentative rather than epigrammatic, and it develops a thought about seva step by step — all features that spurious Gandhi quotes lack, since fabrications tend to be short and quotable. The wording is stable across the citations I recall. I cannot place the source text, so this is a judgment from style and internal evidence rather than from provenance, and I am keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the Collected Works.

The pre-flag is correct. No Gandhi source exists. The earliest credited appearances run through mid-20th-century secondary literature — Louis Fischer's The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) carries a version of the thought as biographer's paraphrase rather than as a transcribed Gandhi sentence — and the line reached mass currency through Attenborough's Gandhi (1982), which drew on Fischer. The underlying reversal of lex talionis is older than Gandhi and circulated independently in English. Fischer is the likeliest proximate source of the wording, but as a paraphraser rather than an author, so I am recording that in notes rather than naming him as the quote's author.

Generally treated as authentic Gandhi and traced to his periodical writing of the early 1930s; the wording is stable across citations and the aphorism-plus-gloss structure matches his editorial style. I cannot name the issue or date, so no print source is given. Held at 0.62 for the standing Gandhi caution — the line is short and quotable, the profile of quotes that drift — but I have no positive evidence against it.

Not a canonical translation. The Majjhima Nikaya credit points at a 152-sutta collection without naming a sutta, and this English does not match any translation tradition I know — not Horner, not Nanamoli/Bodhi. Telltales: 'illusion that he is a permanent self' is a doctrinal gloss on anatta in modern comparative-religion register, not sutta idiom, and the sutta form (address to named interlocutors, formulaic repetition, similes) is entirely absent. This reads as a Western summary of Buddhist teaching later given a scriptural label — a common pattern in inspirational anthologies. Treat the citation as decorative; I cannot identify the actual writer.

Consistently attributed to Malcolm Forbes across quotation collections, and it matches the aphoristic register of his 'Fact and Comment' column in Forbes magazine and the 'Thoughts on the Business of Life' compilations. I cannot place a specific issue, page, or book from training knowledge, so the attribution rests on secondary consistency rather than a primary source. No competing claimant that I know of.

Marc Allen (New World Library founder, author of 'Visionary Business' and 'The Millionaire Course') is a plausible modern popularizer, but the three-tier fool/smart/wise structure is a long-standing proverbial form with many older analogues, notably the aphorism commonly given to Bismarck ('Fools say they learn by experience; I prefer to profit by others' experience') and the 'learn from the mistakes of others, you can't live long enough to make them all yourself' family attributed variously to Eleanor Roosevelt, Groucho Marx, and Hyman Rickover. I cannot confirm that Allen originated this wording, and I will not guess a true source.

results.earliest_print_source: La Prisonniere (The Captive), vol. 5 of A la recherche du temps perdu, Marcel Proust, 1923
results.notes: Genuinely Proust in substance, but this popular English form is a compression, not a translation. The original runs closer to: 'The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others...' ('Le seul veritable voyage... ce ne serait pas d'aller vers de nouveaux paysages, mais d'avoir d'autres yeux'). Source is real and datable; the recorded wording should be understood as a paraphrase.

results.earliest_print_source: Albertine disparue / The Fugitive (also published as The Sweet Cheat Gone), vol. 6 of A la recherche du temps perdu, Marcel Proust, 1925
results.notes: Renders Proust's 'On ne guerit d'une souffrance qu'a condition de l'eprouver pleinement,' from the late volumes of the Recherche dealing with the aftermath of Albertine. I am confident of the author and the work; I am less certain of the exact volume boundary, since the passage is sometimes cited from The Fugitive and sometimes from The Captive. Wording is a standard translation rather than a folk paraphrase.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book VIII, 47 (c. 170-180 CE)
results.notes: Meditations VIII.47. George Long's translation reads 'If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.' The recorded text is that translation modernized in pronouns only; the sense and structure are exact.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book II, 5 (c. 170-180 CE)
results.notes: Condensed from Meditations II.5, commonly rendered 'Perform every act in life as though it were thy last' or 'do everything as if it were the last thing you were doing in your life.' A closely related formulation appears at II.11. Author and work are secure; the recorded line is a shortened translation.

Margaret Gatty (1809-1873), author of 'Parables from Nature' and 'The Book of Sun-Dials' (1872), is the name attached to this line in quotation collections, and the epigrammatic form is consistent with the sundial mottoes she gathered. But I cannot confirm whether she wrote it, translated it, or merely recorded it from an older inscription, and I have no page or edition to cite. Deliberately leaving the print source null rather than guessing at The Book of Sun-Dials.

The well-documented form of this line belongs to John W. Gardner (Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare; founder of Common Cause): 'We are continually faced by great opportunities brilliantly disguised as insoluble problems,' associated with his mid-1960s writing and speeches. The saying has also drifted to Lee Iacocca and Charles Swindoll, and the Margaret Mead version appears in collections without any source in her published anthropological work. I know of no Mead text containing it. Confidence figure reflects the strength of the Mead attribution, which is weak.

Margaret Stortz is a Religious Science / New Thought minister and author, and the sentiment fits that tradition's gratitude-and-attraction idiom, but I have no specific book, article, or sermon in training knowledge that carries this passage. I cannot rule out that it circulates from an anthology or daily-reader compilation. No competing attribution known; the honest answer here is that I cannot place it.

Consistently attributed to Marian Wright Edelman and consistent in voice and content with the numbered life lessons in 'The Measure of Our Success: A Letter to My Children and Yours' (1992), which is where I believe it originates. I am not certain enough of the lesson number or wording in that book to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null. No competing claimant.

results.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 - Text, Ch. 1, 'Principles of Miracles', principle 3
results.notes: This is not original to Marianne Williamson. It is, essentially verbatim, the third of the Fifty Miracle Principles that open the Text of A Course in Miracles: 'Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.' Williamson's 'A Return to Love' (1992) is a commentary on ACIM and quotes the Course extensively, which is how the line came to be tagged with her name. The attribution to her is a quoter-for-author error.
results.suggested_reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)

results.earliest_print_source: A Return to Love: Reflections on the Principles of A Course in Miracles, Marianne Williamson, 1992 (ch. 7)
results.notes: Correctly attributed here, and worth protecting: this passage is one of the most-misattributed texts in circulation, routinely credited to Nelson Mandela's 1994 inaugural address, which does not contain it. Williamson has confirmed authorship. Two wording notes on the recorded text: the original punctuates 'inadequate.' as a full stop before 'Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure,' and the recorded version omits the sentence 'You are a child of God' that follows 'who are you not to be?' - a common secular truncation.

The voice, vocabulary, and subject matter are strongly consistent with Williamson's writing on romantic love, most plausibly 'Enchanted Love: The Mystical Power of Intimate Relationships' (1999) rather than 'A Return to Love.' The ellipses indicate the text was stitched from a longer passage, which is typical of a real book excerpt but also makes it hard to match. I cannot confirm the book or page from training knowledge, so no citation is recorded.

Widely and consistently attributed to Marianne Williamson, and forgiveness-as-world-healing is a central and repeated theme of her work. I cannot locate a specific book or page. One caution given q_0961 in this same batch: Williamson's writing is saturated with A Course in Miracles material, so there is a residual risk that a line like this restates Course teaching; I do not recognize it as verbatim ACIM, but I flag the possibility rather than certify the attribution above the promotion bar.

I believe this comes from Marie-Louise von Franz's chapter 'The Process of Individuation' in 'Man and His Symbols' (C. G. Jung, ed., 1964), which is her best-known writing in English and matches this passage's theme of renewal through attending to the unconscious. The editorial bracket '[of renewal]' suggests the corpus entry was taken from a careful print quotation rather than a meme. I am not confident enough of the chapter or page to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null and the attribution rests on style and subject match plus consistent secondary citation.

Consistently attributed to Marilyn Ferguson, author of 'The Aquarian Conspiracy' (1980) and editor of the Brain/Mind Bulletin, and the framing of fear as information matches her idiom. The passage's length and structure suggest an excerpt from her writing rather than an aphorism assembled by anthologists. I cannot confirm the book or issue, so no citation is recorded.

One of the most-reproduced lines credited to Marilyn Ferguson, with consistent attribution but, as far as I know, no cited source anywhere in that circulation. Short aphorisms of this kind are the ones most likely to be detached from an author or absorbed from workshop culture, so consistent repetition is weak evidence on its own. Plausibly hers - it reads like a condensation of the same material as q_0966 - but unverified.

Solidly and consistently attributed to Mario Andretti in interviews and racing literature, though I cannot name the original interview or date. Important wording caveat: the canonical form is 'If everything seems under control, you're not going fast enough.' The recorded text ('feels under control ... just not driving fast enough') is a drifted variant. Recommend normalizing to the standard wording before promotion.

results.earliest_print_source: The Innocents Abroad, Mark Twain, 1869 (Conclusion)
results.notes: Genuine Twain, from the closing chapter of The Innocents Abroad: 'Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry, and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things cannot be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one's lifetime.' The recorded entry is lowercased and truncated mid-sentence; it should be capitalized and either closed with a period or extended to the full clause.

The pre-flag is correct. No such line appears in Twain's published work, letters, or notebooks, and the attributions to him begin decades after his death in 1910 - the earliest instance I know of is a 1970 John Robert Colombo 'found poem' that presents 'History never repeats itself but it rhymes' as a Twain saying, which is a repetition of the claim rather than evidence for it. I cannot identify a true originator, so no reattribution is offered; classifying as apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed for exactly that reason. See also q_0975, a near-duplicate of this entry.

The pre-flag is correct: no source in Twain's published work or correspondence. The same sentence circulates just as often under Ralph Waldo Emerson's name, and that attribution is equally unsourced - Emerson's actual related line, from 'Heroism,' is 'Always do what you are afraid to do,' which he credits to his aunt Mary Moody Emerson. Because both major claimants fail and I cannot identify a real origin, apocryphal with no reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Pudd'nhead Wilson, Mark Twain, 1894 - epigraph to ch. 12, from 'Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar'
results.notes: Genuine Twain, unlike the three neighbouring entries in this batch. It appears as a Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar epigraph and continues '...except a creature that has no fear, in which case courage would be meaningless.' The original punctuates with a dash: 'Courage is resistance to fear, mastery of fear - not absence of fear.' The recorded comma is a minor deviation.

results.earliest_print_source: P.S. I Love You, H. Jackson Brown Jr., 1990
results.notes: The pre-flag matches what I know. Nothing in Twain's corpus contains this, and 'throw off the bowlines / sail away from the safe harbor' is not his register. The earliest documented appearance is in H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 'P.S. I Love You' (1990), a collection of sayings from his mother, Sarah Frances Brown; the Twain tag attached afterwards and spread through 1990s self-help and graduation-speech material. Recording the true origin here because it is documented, not inferred - but note that Brown's book presents it as his mother's saying, so 'H. Jackson Brown Jr.' is the compiler rather than strictly the author.
results.suggested_reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)

results.notes: Not pre-flagged, but it should have been. No Twain source exists for this. It is a wordy variant of the unsourced 'Worrying is like paying a debt you don't owe,' which circulates under Twain, Will Rogers, and others without a citation for any of them. The one genuinely documented aphorism in this family belongs to William Ralph Inge, Dean of St Paul's: 'Worry is interest paid on trouble before it falls due.' The recorded wording differs enough that I will not reattribute it to Inge, but his line is the likely ancestor of the metaphor. Recommend flagging this entry as suspect.

Same verdict as q_0970, of which this is a near-duplicate differing only by the word 'does' - the corpus is carrying both variants and should deduplicate. No Twain source; attributions post-date his 1910 death by decades, with the earliest I know of being John Robert Colombo's 1970 found poem. No identifiable true author, hence apocryphal with no reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Mark Twain's Notebook, ed. Albert Bigelow Paine, 1935
results.notes: Genuine Twain, from a notebook entry (c. 1904) first published posthumously in Mark Twain's Notebook (1935). Usual wording is 'Whenever you find yourself on the side of the majority...'. Not from a work published in his lifetime, so the chain runs through Paine's edited notebooks rather than a primary printed text — hence attributed rather than verified.

results.earliest_print_source: "What Paul Bourget Thinks of Us", North American Review, 1895; collected in How to Tell a Story and Other Essays, 1897
results.notes: Genuine Twain essay line. The original reads closer to 'Humor is the great thing, the saving thing after all. The minute it crops up, all our hardnesses yield, all our irritations and resentments flit away, and a sunny spirit takes their place.' The corpus text is a slightly condensed variant, and it carries a stray trailing double-quote character that should be stripped in normalization.

results.earliest_print_source: The Mysterious Stranger, Mark Twain, 1916 (posthumous)
results.notes: The idea is genuinely Twain's, from the Satan monologue in the Mysterious Stranger manuscripts: the human race 'has unquestionably one really effective weapon - laughter.' The exact sentence as quoted here is a smoothed condensation rather than Twain's printed wording, and the 1916 text itself was editorially assembled by Paine and Duneka from Twain's drafts. Correct author, imprecise wording.

Not found in Twain's works or letters; Twain attributions for this line are late and unsupported. The 'if you don't mind, it doesn't matter' pun on mind/matter circulated as a stock joke well before it was pinned to any famous name. It is most commonly credited to Satchel Paige ('Age is a question of mind over matter...'), but Paige popularized rather than originated it, so I am not asserting a replacement author.

results.earliest_print_source: Mark Twain's Notebook, ed. Albert Bigelow Paine, 1935 (entry dated 1894)
results.notes: Genuine Twain notebook entry, consistently cited to the 1894 notebooks published in 1935. Attributed rather than verified because the source is Paine's posthumous edited compilation rather than a text Twain saw into print.

I cannot place this in any Twain text - not in the novels, essays, letters, or notebooks I know. It reads like a newspaper-filler aphorism that later collected a Twain byline, the standard pattern for spurious Twain. I do not have a confident true origin, so I am recording honest uncertainty rather than a reattribution.

A classic spurious Twain. It appears in no Twain work; documented appearances postdate his 1910 death, and it is biographically impossible as autobiography - John Marshall Clemens died when Samuel Clemens was eleven, so there was no father to rediscover at twenty-one. Origin unknown; the joke circulated anonymously in periodicals before acquiring Twain's name.

results.earliest_print_source: Mark Twain's Notebook, ed. Albert Bigelow Paine, 1935
results.notes: Same Twain notebook entry as q_0976, in the more common 'find yourself / it's time' wording - these two records are duplicates of one quote and one of them should be dropped in dedup. Genuine Twain, sourced to the posthumously published notebooks rather than a lifetime imprint.

results.earliest_print_source: The Mysterious Stranger, Mark Twain, 1916, ch. 10
results.notes: Genuine, from Satan's closing speech on laughter as the human race's one effective weapon. Caveat: the 1916 published Mysterious Stranger was stitched together and partly rewritten by Paine and Duneka from Twain's unfinished manuscripts, but this sentence is present in Twain's own drafting of that passage.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter from Mark Twain to Mrs. Foote, 2 December 1887
results.notes: Genuine Twain, from an 1887 letter; the original phrasing is 'all you need in this life is ignorance and confidence, and then success is sure.' The corpus drops 'this' from 'in this life' - minor variance, correct author and traceable primary document.

No Twain source known to me. The vocation/vacation pun circulates in several forms ('Make your vocation your vacation') attached to various names, and I cannot trace any of them to a document. Twain's name here looks like the usual gravitational pull of a famous humorist on an unowned wordplay.

Consistently attributed to Twain across quote collections and stylistically plausible for him; I have a weak recollection of it sitting in one of the late novels but cannot place the work or chapter with enough confidence to name it, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Author plausible, citation unconfirmed.

Widely printed over Twain's name but absent from his writings so far as I know; the Twain attribution surfaces decades after his death, and quote-tracing work on this line has failed to find any contemporaneous support. Related sentiments about kindness as a universal language predate the Twain version. True origin unknown to me.

results.earliest_print_source: Following the Equator, Mark Twain, 1897 (epigraph from Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar)
results.notes: Genuine Twain, one of the Pudd'nhead Wilson's New Calendar chapter epigraphs in Following the Equator. Twain's wording is 'the full value of a joy'; the corpus reads 'of joy'. Correct author, published in his lifetime.

Very consistently attributed to Twain and usually pointed at his notebooks, but I cannot confirm which entry or letter, and I have not seen it quoted with a page citation. Plausible but unconfirmed - keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the notebooks.

results.earliest_print_source: "The Computer for the 21st Century", Mark Weiser, Scientific American, September 1991
results.notes: These are the opening two sentences of Weiser's ubiquitous-computing paper, quoted verbatim and correctly. One of the best-documented attributions in computing; the text matches the published article word for word.

results.earliest_print_source: Reflexions et maximes, Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues, 1746
results.notes: The maxim is Vauvenargues': 'Il n'est rien que la peur ne fasse croire,' from his Reflexions et maximes (published 1746 with the Introduction a la connaissance de l'esprit humain). The author field is misspelled and mistitled - it should read 'Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues', not 'Marquis de Vauvengras'. I am confident of the author, less so of the exact maxim number, so I have not cited one.
results.suggested_reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)

results.notes: Consistently credited to the playwright Marsha Norman with no competing claimants, and it circulated widely after appearing in magazine quote features in the 1990s. I cannot name the interview, play, or essay it came from, so the citation stays null. Author likely right, source unlocated.

Attributed to Marsha Sinetar, whose subject matter (right livelihood, mind-body integration, contemplative practice) fits the content well - most likely from one of her books such as Do What You Love, the Money Will Follow (1987) or Ordinary People as Monks and Mystics (1986), but I cannot confirm which and will not guess a title.

Attributed to Marsha Sinetar in quote collections; the water-and-obstacle imagery reads like her commentary on an I Ching hexagram, which is consistent with her writing, but I cannot place the book or page. The ellipsis in the text indicates it is already an excerpt from a longer passage, which makes verification harder rather than easier.

results.earliest_print_source: Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life, Marshall B. Rosenberg, PuddleDancer Press, 1999 (2nd ed. 2003)
results.notes: Genuine Rosenberg, from the opening chapter of Nonviolent Communication, where he introduces observation/feeling/need as the alternative to diagnosis and judgment. Wording and vocabulary match the book directly. Confident in book and author; I have not pinned an exact page.

Widely and consistently credited to McLuhan, but I know of no primary citation - no book, lecture, or interview I can point to. Complicating it: 'Spaceship Earth' is Buckminster Fuller's frame (Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, 1969), and the line is sometimes handed to Fuller instead. McLuhan is the more common attribution and is plausible, but the evidence I have is secondary repetition, not a source.

Genuine-sounding Graham and consistently attributed to her, from her writing on modern dance in the 1930s-50s. Note a probable transcription corruption: the standard wording is 'We look FOR the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life,' not 'look at the dance.' I cannot name the essay or collection with confidence, so no citation.

results.earliest_print_source: Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham, Agnes de Mille, Random House, 1991
results.notes: The famous 'keep the channel open' passage, spoken by Graham to Agnes de Mille and recorded by de Mille in her Graham biography. Important caveat for the corpus: this is de Mille's written recollection of Graham's spoken words, not text Graham published, and the widely circulated version has drifted slightly from de Mille's page. Also note the typo carried in this record: 'this expression in unique' should read 'is unique'.

A variant rendering of the same de Mille conversation behind q_0999 ('because there is only one of you in all time'). It circulates as a standalone Graham line, but I cannot match it word for word to de Mille's text, so it may be a paraphrase in transmission rather than a distinct utterance. Author right, exact wording unverified.
